formulary.indications:
i)Treatment of Herpes simplex & Varicella zoster infections

ii)Prophylaxis of Herpes simplex infections in immune-compromised patients
formulary.dose:
ADULT: 5 mg/kg by IV infusion 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 10mg/kg every 8 hourly in varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for at least 10 days in encephalitis; possibly for 14 - 21 days). 

NEONATE & INFANT up to 3 months with disseminated herpes simplex: 20mg/kg every 8 hourly for 14 days (21 days in CNS involvement), varicella-zoster 10-20mg/kg every 8 hourly usually for 7 days. 

CHILD, 3 months - 12 years: Herpes simplex or Varicella Zoster: 250 mg/m2 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 500 mg/m2 8 hourly for varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for 10 days in encephalitis)

entries.indications:
i)Treatment of Herpes simplex & Varicella zoster infections

ii)Prophylaxis of Herpes simplex infections in immune-compromised patients
entries.dose:
Indication (i)
Treatment for Herpes Simplex: ADULT - 200mg 5 times daily; In severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg. CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Treatment for Varicella Zoster: ADULT - 800mg 5 times daily; CHILD - 6 years and over: 800 mg four times daily, 2 - < 6 years: 400 mg four times daily, Under 2 years: 200 mg four times daily.

Indication (ii)
ADULT - Immune-compromised patients: 200 mg four times daily. Severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg.
CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Dosing is according to Product Information Leaflet.

entries.interactions: Increased mean half-life & plasma concentration with probenecid
entries.precautions: Patients with pre-existing neurologic, renal, or hepatic impairment, dehydrated patient, elderly and lactation

preparation.reconstitution: 250 mg vial: reconstitute with 10 mL WFI or NS to 25 mg/mL.
preparation.dilution: Further dilute to a concentration not greater than 5 mg/mL. For adults, 100 mL infusion bags are used; a second bag is needed for doses >500 mg up to 1 g.

preparation.comments: Discard if turbidity or crystallisation develops; too-rapid infusion may damage renal tubules.

clinicalReconciliation.title: High-risk reconciliation — aminoglycoside/TDM
clinicalReconciliation.summary: Aminoglycosides require concentration-aware dosing. Routine EID/SDD is not appropriate in several NAG-listed populations.
points: NAG EID/SDD exclusions include pregnancy, endocarditis, CrCl <30 mL/min, dialysis and haemodynamic instability among others.
MSIC provides timed concentration sampling and recommends more frequent monitoring with changing renal function/nephrotoxins.
AbxHub does not automatically calculate a maintenance interval from a single creatinine clearance value for high-risk aminoglycoside use.

clinicalReconciliation.title: Adult/ICU RRT vs neonatal NAG schedules
clinicalReconciliation.summary: MSIC adult RRT dosing and NAG neonatal/paediatric dosing are preserved as separate source layers.
points: MSIC adult ICU appendix provides HD/CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF schedules with TDM.
NAG neonatal pathways use 15 mg/kg with CGA-specific q24–48h intervals.
NAG paediatric pyelonephritis lists 15 mg/kg IV daily when amikacin is selected.

entries.adverseReactions: Transient and reversible reticulocytopaenia, drug fever, rash, bradycardia, transient 1st-degree heart block and reversible elevation of serum transaminases.
entries.contraindications: Artesunate is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to artesunate or other artemisinins.

entries.precautions: Hepatic or renal insufficiency. Pregnancy and lactation.

entries.adverseReactions: Nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Headache and skin rash. Reversible hearing loss. Alteration of sense of smell with taste perversion. Glossitis, stomatitis, oral monilia, tongue discoloration, tooth discoloration (reversible), liver failure, immune hypersensitivity reaction (severe), anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs)
entries.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to macrolides. Patients receiving terfenadine therapy with pre-existing cardiac abnormalities or electrolyte disturbances. Concomitant cisapride, pimozide, astemizole, terfenadine, ergotamine or dihydroergotamine. Concomitant administration of clarithromycin and domperidone as this may result in QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias including ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation and torsades de pointes.
entries.interactions: Modest increase of circulating theophylline or carbamazepine levels. May potentiate effects of warfarin or digoxin. May alter metabolism of terfenadine resulting in increased levels of terfenadine. Inhibition of metabolism with ritonavir. Co-administration of clarithromycin and a drug primarily metabolized by CYP3A may be associated with elevation in drug concentrations that could increase or prolong both therapeutic and adverse effects of the concomitant drug.
entries.precautions: Impaired hepatic function and moderate to severe renal impairment. Absence of proven or strongly suspected infection; increased risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Acute porphyria, history of concomitant therapy with ranitidine, bismuth citrate therapy is not recommended Pseudomembranous colitis may occur; consider this diagnosis in patients who develop diarrhea during therapy . Renal impairment, severe; dosage adjustment needed; when CrCl is less than 25 mL/min, concurrent use of ranitidine bismuth citrate is not recommended.

formulary.indications: Intravenous administration for the treatment of serious infections caused by Gram negative bacteria, when more commonly used systemic antibacterial agents may be contraindicated or may be ineffective because of bacterial resistance.
formulary.dose:
A minimum of 5 days treatment is generally recommended. For the treatment of respiratory exacerbations in cystic fibrosis patients, treatment should be continued up to 12 days. 

Children and adults (including elderly): 
Up to 60kg: 50,000 units/kg/day to a maximum of 75,000 units/kg/day. The total daily dose should be divided into three doses given at approximately 8-hour intervals. 
Over 60kg: 1-2 million units three times a day. The maximum dose is 6 million units in 24 hours. 

Renal impairment: 
In moderate to severe renal impairment, excretion of colistimethate sodium is delayed. 
Dosage in Renal Impairment (for over 60 kg body weight): 
- Mild (CrCl 20-50 ml/min): 1-2 million units every 8 hr. 
- Moderate (CrCl 10-20 ml/min): 1 million units every 12-18 hr. 
- Severe (CrCl <10 ml/min): 1 million units every 18-24 hr.

entries.adverseReactions:
- Apnoea, transient sensory disturbances (such as facial paraesthesia and vertigo) and rarely, vasomotor instability, slurred speech, visual disturbances, confusion or psychosis. 
- Nephrotoxicity reported following the use of higher than recommended doses or failure to reduce the dosage in patients with renal impairment or during concomitant use of other nephrotoxic drugs. 
- Hypersensitivity reactions such as rash, drug fever. 
- Local irritation at injection site.
entries.contraindications:
- Hypersensitivity to colistimethate or polymyxin B. 
- Myasthenia gravis.
entries.interactions: Aminoglycoside such as gentamicin, amikacin, netilmicin, tobramycin and neuromuscular blocking drugs.
entries.precautions:
- Patients with porphyria, renal impairment. 
- Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and bronchospam may occur. 
- Monitor serum colistimethate sodium concentration. 
- May affect ability to drive or operate machinery as neurotoxicity may occur with the possibility of dizziness, confusion or visual disturbances.

paediatric.blueBookDose:
A minimum of 5 days treatment is generally recommended. For the treatment of respiratory exacerbations in cystic fibrosis patients, treatment should be continued up to 12 days. 

Children and adults (including elderly): 
Up to 60kg: 50,000 units/kg/day to a maximum of 75,000 units/kg/day. The total daily dose should be divided into three doses given at approximately 8-hour intervals. 
Over 60kg: 1-2 million units three times a day. The maximum dose is 6 million units in 24 hours. 

Renal impairment: 
In moderate to severe renal impairment, excretion of colistimethate sodium is delayed. 
Dosage in Renal Impairment (for over 60 kg body weight): 
- Mild (CrCl 20-50 ml/min): 1-2 million units every 8 hr. 
- Moderate (CrCl 10-20 ml/min): 1 million units every 12-18 hr. 
- Severe (CrCl <10 ml/min): 1 million units every 18-24 hr.

- Metoclopramide can decrease levels in urine and should be avoided. 
- Probenecid can decrease renal clearance and excretion of fosfomycin and should be avoided.
entries.precautions:
- Moderate renal impairment. 
- Elderly.

precautions: Restrict topical therapy to appropriate localised indications and duration.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to fusidic acid/fusidates; additional contraindications are formulation-specific.
interactions: Systemic fusidic acid has clinically important interaction potential; verify current product information, particularly with hepatotoxic/myotoxic co-medications.

entries.precautions:
Fluoroquinolone are associated with an increased risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture in all the age; especially older patients, patient taking corticosteroid drugs and patient with kidney, heart or lung transplants. Caution in infusion rate, a rapid or bolus IV may result hypotension. Renal impairment (CrCl less than 50 mL/minute), CNS disorders, predisposition to seizures, lowered convulsion threshold, diabetes mellitus, conditions predisposing to torsade de pointes, significant bradycardia, cardiomyopathy, G6PD deficiency. Ensure adequate hydration. Avoid excessive sun exposure. May affect ability to drive or operate machinery.

Aortic aneurysm and dissection: Fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in patients with positive family history of aneurysm disease, or in patients diagnosed with pre-existing aortic aneurysm and/or aortic dissection, or in presence of other risk factors or conditions predisposing for aortic aneurysm and dissection (e.g. Marfan syndrome, vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Takayasu arteritis, giant cell arteritis, Behcet's disease, hypertension, known artherosclerosis). In case of sudden abdominal, chest or back pain, patients should be advised to immediately consult a physician in an emergency department.

entries.adverseReactions: Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, pyrexia, mucosal inflammation, rigors, peripheral oedema, fatigue, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, anorexia, hyperglycaemia, fluid overload, bacteraemia, sepsis, cough, dyspnea, epitaxis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anaemia, febrile neutropenia, rash, pruritus, headache, insomnia, anxiety, hypotension, hypertension, phlebitis, back pain, tachycardia.
entries.contraindications: Micafungin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to any component of this medication or to other echinocandins.
entries.interactions: Micafungin has a low potential for interactions with medicines metabolised via CYP3A mediated pathway. However, patients receiving sirolimus, nifedipine or itraconazole in combination with micafungin should be monitored for toxicity and the dosage of sirolimus, nifedipine or itraconazole should be reduced if necessary.
entries.precautions:
Hypersensitivity: Anaphylactic / anaphylactoid reactions including shock may occur. 
Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorder: Exfoliative cutaneous reactions, such as Steven-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrosis have been reported. 
Haemolysis: Isolated cases of haemolysis including acute intravascular haemolysis or haemolytic anaemia have been reported. 
Hepatic effects: Early discontinuation in the presence of significant and persistent elevation of ALT / AST is recommended. Micafungin treatment should be conducted on a careful risk/benefit basis, particularly in patients having severe liver function impairment or chronic liver diseases. 
Use in pregnancy: There are no adequate or well-controlled studies of micafungin in pregnant women. 
Use in lactation: Caution should be exercised when micafungin is administered during breastfeeding. 
Use in the elderly: No dose adjustment is necessary for the elderly.

clinicalReconciliation.title: High-risk reconciliation — vancomycin/TDM
clinicalReconciliation.summary: NAG and MSIC both support exposure-guided monitoring. AbxHub keeps NAG monitoring principles and MSIC ICU renal/RRT schedules visibly separate.
points: NAG: AUC/MIC is the efficacy exposure metric; Bayesian estimation is described as gold standard, with a two-level analytic alternative.
NAG: TDM when therapy is expected >48 h; at least biweekly monitoring when clinically stable.
MSIC: source-specific loading, renal/RRT regimens and sampling schedules remain linked; do not convert this into an unvalidated one-level AUC calculator.

clinicalReconciliation.title: Current NAG + MSIC vancomycin/TDM reconciliation
clinicalReconciliation.summary: Current NAG defines AUC-guided monitoring principles; MSIC provides ICU loading/renal/RRT examples. AbxHub does not collapse these into an unvalidated automatic AUC prescription.
points: NAG: AUC is estimated by Bayesian software (gold standard) or a two-concentration analytic approach; TDM is indicated when therapy is expected >48 h.
MSIC: AUC0–24/MIC target 400–600 is listed in the ICU appendix and its CRRT example changes maintenance by MIC and effluent rate.
Use the local validated assay timing/Bayesian platform and reassess whenever renal function, RRT prescription or haemodynamics change.

conditions.summary: Trauma-specific gateway separating no-antibiotic situations from operative hollow-viscus contamination and established infection.

preferred: No systemic antibiotics are required solely for abdominal trauma when no operation is performed.

conditions.name: Acute Appendicitis / Appendiceal Infection
conditions.summary: Source control defines the antibiotic course; postoperative antibiotics can often stop after adequate source control in uncomplicated disease.
before: Assess uncomplicated vs perforated/abscess disease

recommendations.label: Uncomplicated — non-operative management
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5–3 g IV q8h
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Total 7–10 days IV + PO with close clinical monitoring; switch to oral when improving and re-evaluate for surgery if symptoms do not resolve.

recommendations.label: After appendectomy with adequate uncomplicated source control
preferred: Antibiotics may be stopped once surgery has achieved adequate source control and symptoms have resolved.
recommendations.duration: No routine prolonged postoperative course when uncomplicated source control is adequate.

recommendations.label: Complicated appendicitis — abscess/perforation/peritonitis
preferred: Non-sepsis: amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5–3 g IV q8h
Sepsis/organ failure: piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Non-sepsis: ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h OR cefoperazone 1–2 g IV q12h, plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Use a short source-control-directed course and individualise to adequacy of drainage/surgery and clinical response.

why: Duration should follow source control rather than an automatic prolonged course.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Barrier disruption, obstruction, perforation or infected fluid collections expose normally sterile sites to enteric organisms; source control is a major determinant of cure.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Prioritise source-control imaging/procedure where indicated and culture normally sterile intra-abdominal/biliary/abscess material when obtained.
Blood cultures are useful in sepsis; avoid overinterpreting cultures from chronically placed drains.

notes: When piperacillin/tazobactam is given q8h, NAG specifies extended infusion over 3–4 h.

recommendations.duration: 7–10 days in the source table; 4–7 days after adequate source control in the source-listed scenarios.

conditions.summary: Most uncomplicated community watery diarrhoea is managed primarily with rehydration; antimicrobial therapy is reserved for selected severity, host-risk and pathogen-directed situations.
before: Assess dehydration, sepsis, bloody stool, travel/outbreak exposure and immunocompromise.
Prioritise oral/IV fluid and electrolyte replacement.
Avoid reflex empirical antibiotics for uncomplicated self-limiting watery diarrhoea.

recommendations.label: Acute severe infectious diarrhoea
preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV q12h for 3–5 days; optional azithromycin 1 g single dose OR doxycycline 300 mg single dose when Vibrio cholerae is suspected.
alternative: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h for 3 days.
recommendations.duration: Empirical table 3–5 days; MSIC notes salmonellosis 7–14 days when confirmed.
notes: MSIC advises no antimicrobial therapy for clinically stable mild–moderate disease without hypovolaemia.
Consider empirical treatment for severe hypovolaemia, immunocompromise, high fever/severe symptoms or bloody diarrhoea.

recommendations.label: Bloody diarrhoea
preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV q12h for 3–5 days.
alternative: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h for 3 days.
If Entamoeba histolytica dysentery is suspected: metronidazole 750 mg IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: Shigella dysentery 7–10 days in immunocompromised patients; amoebic dysentery 7–10 days.

why: Rehydration is the main treatment for uncomplicated acute watery diarrhoea.

conditions.name: Aspiration Pneumonia
conditions.summary: Distinguish aspiration pneumonitis from bacterial aspiration infection; syndrome and healthcare exposure determine whether broad Gram-negative/anaerobic coverage is needed.
before: Obtain appropriate cultures before antimicrobials when this does not cause harmful delay
Review previous microbiology and recent antimicrobial exposure
Check allergy and previous serious antimicrobial adverse reactions
Check renal function and whether renal replacement therapy is being used
Assess for abscess/empyema and need for drainage
Clarify community vs healthcare-associated aspiration

recommendations.label: Local aspiration pneumonia
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h ± metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days in the HPUSM table.

recommendations.label: Healthcare-associated aspiration / lung abscess
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
alternative: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h
recommendations.duration: Aspiration pneumonia 7 days; lung abscess minimum 4 weeks

recommendations.label: Aspiration pneumonia (not chemical pneumonitis)
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h ± metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h when anaerobic coverage is specifically indicated
β-lactam allergy: clindamycin 600 mg IV/PO q8h
recommendations.duration: 7 days. Routine anaerobic coverage is not required unless lung abscess/empyema is suspected.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Microbial infection of airways/alveoli triggers local inflammatory exudate and impaired gas exchange; aspiration, ventilation, host defence and resistance risk determine likely pathogens.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain a quality respiratory specimen for microscopy/culture when disease is severe, hospital-acquired or treatment failure/MDR is a concern.
Blood cultures are appropriate in severe/systemic illness; interpret respiratory growth with colonisation risk and clinical/radiologic findings.

conditions.name: Bacterial / Endogenous Endophthalmitis
conditions.summary: Sight-threatening endophthalmitis requires immediate ophthalmology/vitreoretinal management. Post-operative/post-traumatic and endogenous pathways have different systemic recommendations; both require source/microbiology review.
before: Immediate ophthalmology/vitreoretinal review.
Obtain vitreous/aqueous and systemic cultures as appropriate; search for primary endogenous source.

recommendations.label: Post-operative / post-traumatic bacterial endophthalmitis
preferred: Intravitreal vancomycin 1–2 mg/0.1 mL + ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 mL
For severe/virulent disease or delayed transfer: systemic vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (max 2 g/dose) + ceftazidime 1–2 g IV q8h
alternative: Intravitreal vancomycin + amikacin; selected systemic oral ciprofloxacin/moxifloxacin alternatives are source-listed
recommendations.duration: Repeat intravitreal therapy after 48–72 h if indicated. Systemic antibiotics, when required, are typically 2–4 weeks and up to 6 weeks depending on ophthalmologic response.

recommendations.label: Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis
preferred: Systemic ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h OR cefotaxime 2 g IV q4h + intravitreal vancomycin 1–2 mg/0.1 mL + ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 mL
alternative: Culture-negative: add clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h for 7–14 days; selected systemic ciprofloxacin/moxifloxacin and intravitreal amikacin alternatives are source-listed
recommendations.duration: Systemic therapy is source/primary-infection dependent and commonly 2–4 weeks up to 6 weeks; review microbiology and ophthalmologic response.

why: Review microbiology promptly and de-escalate/redirect; fungal endophthalmitis requires a separate antifungal pathway.

conditions.name: Bacterial Meningitis
conditions.summary: Time-critical syndrome: obtain blood cultures/CSF when safe without delaying treatment. Dose selection must achieve CNS exposure.
before: Obtain blood cultures promptly
Perform lumbar puncture when safe; do not delay time-critical antimicrobials for prolonged investigations
Assess need for imaging before LP based on neurological features
Consider age/immunocompromise and Listeria risk

recommendations.label: Adult empirical local regimen
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + ampicillin 2 g IV q4h
alternative: Use allergy/pathogen-specific regimen
recommendations.duration: 7–21 days depending on organism/clinical context
notes: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h for 2–4 days is listed in the source.

recommendations.label: Adult acute bacterial meningitis — empirical
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + ampicillin 2 g IV q4h when Listeria coverage is indicated
alternative: Cefotaxime 2 g IV q6h + ampicillin 2 g IV q4h
Severe cephalosporin allergy: consider meropenem 2 g IV q8h

recommendations.duration: Acyclovir 14 days for specified exposure; antibacterial prophylaxis/treatment as above.

recommendations.label: Posterior blepharitis / meibomian gland dysfunction
preferred: Warm compresses and massage; systemic therapy is not initial treatment.
alternative: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q24h or q12h for 4–6 weeks; NAG also lists azithromycin pulse therapy.

recommendations.label: Local empirical regimen
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
alternative: Cefotaxime 2 g IV q4–6h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 4–8 weeks; source lists minimum 2 weeks IV

recommendations.label: Oral / sinus / haematogenous source
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h OR cefotaxime 2 g IV q4–6h, PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Usually 4–8 weeks; NAG specifies at least 2 weeks IV, then duration depends on drainage, clinical response and radiological response.
notes: De-escalate according to culture and susceptibility.

recommendations.label: Otogenic source
preferred: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h, PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Usually 4–8 weeks with at least 2 weeks IV; individualise by drainage and clinical/radiological response.

Blood cultures may identify a haematogenous source.

recommendations.duration: 7–10 days in the local table; definitive duration depends on organism and clinical context.

notes: HPUSM suggests catheter removal; use vancomycin TDM and syndrome-specific S. aureus bacteraemia/endocarditis rules when applicable.

recommendations.label: Non-tunnelled central venous catheter / PICC — national empirical pathway

recommendations.duration: Depends on organism, catheter removal and complications; NAG suggests ID consultation.

recommendations.duration: Single systemic ceftriaxone dose per NAG ocular pathway; manage STI contacts/systemic infection separately.

before: Start rapid oral/IV fluid and electrolyte replacement

preferred: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Ampicillin 2 g IV q6h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h; for caesarean delivery add metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Continue postpartum until afebrile and asymptomatic for at least 48 h; NAG notes no proven benefit from routine oral continuation after parenteral therapy is stopped.

recommendations.label: Antibiotic allergy
preferred: Mild allergy: cefazolin 2 g IV q8h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h
alternative: Severe allergy: clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Continue postpartum until afebrile/asymptomatic for at least 48 h.

conditions.name: Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis
conditions.summary: Requires a prolonged prostate-penetrating, susceptibility-directed regimen.
before: Obtain urine/culture evidence when possible
Review STI/atypical pathogen context and prior courses

recommendations.label: Culture-directed chronic prostatitis
preferred: Ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg PO q12h for 4–6 weeks
alternative: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg PO q12h for 4–12 weeks
Doxycycline 100 mg PO q24h for 10 days only for C. trachomatis/mycoplasma infection
Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 weeks only for the source-specified pathogen context
recommendations.duration: 4–6 weeks for ciprofloxacin; alternative durations as listed above.
notes: Urology review is recommended to distinguish chronic bacterial from non-bacterial prostatitis.

why: Short courses have a high relapse risk because prostatic infection is difficult to eradicate.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Most bacterial urinary infections ascend from periurethral flora; obstruction, instrumentation, stones and prostate involvement can promote persistence, bacteraemia and sepsis.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained before antibiotics when systemic/complicated infection is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness and evaluate obstruction, stones, catheter or abscess where relevant.

conditions.name: Clostridioides difficile Infection
conditions.summary: Stop unnecessary inciting antimicrobials when possible and classify severity; fulminant disease requires high-dose oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole in the NAG pathway.
before: Stop or narrow inciting antimicrobial when clinically feasible
Assess WCC, creatinine, shock, ileus and megacolon
Institute infection-control precautions according to local policy

recommendations.label: Initial non-severe / severe
preferred: Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h
alternative: Non-severe only: metronidazole 400 mg PO q8h if vancomycin unavailable
recommendations.duration: 10 days.

recommendations.label: Fulminant colitis
preferred: Vancomycin 500 mg PO q6h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Urgent reassessment and source-control/surgical evaluation according to clinical course.

recommendations.label: Non-severe / severe CDI
preferred: Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h.
recommendations.duration: 10 days.
notes: Source severity markers: WBC <15×10^9/L and creatinine <132 μmol/L for non-severe; WBC ≥15×10^9/L and creatinine >132 μmol/L for severe.

recommendations.label: Fulminant CDI
preferred: Vancomycin 500 mg PO q6h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h.
alternative: If ileus: consider rectal vancomycin 500 mg in 100 mL normal saline q6h by enema.
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days.
notes: Fulminant CDI in MSIC: shock with peritonitis, ileus or megacolon.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Antibiotic-mediated microbiome disruption permits toxigenic C. difficile expansion; toxin-mediated epithelial injury produces diarrhoea, colitis and potentially fulminant disease.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Test diarrhoeal stool using the local toxin/NAAT algorithm; do not test formed stool or use a positive molecular test alone without compatible symptoms.

Open/penetrating injury without dural breach: cefazolin or cefuroxime ± metronidazole; amoxicillin/clavulanate is an alternative pathway.
Prophylaxis ends by 24 h after closure or 72 h total, whichever occurs first, in the cited pathway.

conditions.name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia — Non-severe Adult
conditions.summary: Confirm radiographic/clinical CAP and use severity/comorbidity to choose outpatient versus inpatient treatment; TB and prior healthcare/antibiotic exposure must be considered.
before: Confirm compatible syndrome plus infiltrate and consider alternative diagnoses/TB.
Assess CURB-65/SMART-COP and comorbidities, allergy, prior antibiotics and local susceptibility.

recommendations.label: HPUSM mild–moderate CAP (CURB65 0–1)
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days in the HPUSM CAP table.

recommendations.label: HPUSM moderate CAP (CURB65 2–3)
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h PLUS azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h PLUS azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days in the HPUSM CAP table.

recommendations.label: Outpatient — no relevant comorbidity
preferred: Amoxicillin 500–1000 mg PO q8h
alternative: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days, guided by clinical stability.

recommendations.label: Outpatient — comorbidities
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h; add azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 days or doxycycline when atypical coverage is indicated
alternative: Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h for severe beta-lactam allergy/selected situations
recommendations.duration: Amoxicillin/clavulanate/doxycycline 5–7 days; azithromycin 3 days; levofloxacin 5 days.

recommendations.label: Moderate inpatient CAP
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h ± azithromycin/doxycycline
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h ± azithromycin; allergy: levofloxacin 750 mg IV/PO q24h
recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days, with IV→PO switch when clinically appropriate.

why: Use the existing Severe CAP pathway for high-severity disease.

conditions.name: Complicated Intra-Abdominal Infection
conditions.summary: Early source control plus appropriate antimicrobial therapy are the core management principles.
before: Obtain blood cultures in septic patients
Obtain operative/peritoneal specimens when source control is performed
Assess whether infection is community- or hospital-acquired
Prioritise source control

recommendations.label: Principle
preferred: Use narrower therapy for community-acquired IAI when appropriate; hospital-acquired IAI more often requires MDR-aware coverage
alternative: Tailor to local epidemiology and culture
recommendations.duration: After adequate source control, duration should be limited and response-driven

recommendations.label: Complicated diverticulitis / appendicitis phenotype — national pathway
preferred: Non-sepsis: amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ampicillin–sulbactam 1.5–3 g IV q6h
Sepsis / organ failure: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Non-sepsis: ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h OR cefoperazone 1–2 g IV q12h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Complicated appendicitis: 4–7 days when adequate source control is achieved and recovery is rapid; reserve carbapenem for high AMR risk.
notes: If piperacillin–tazobactam is given q8h, NAG specifies extended infusion over 3–4 h.
Source control remains central.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Prioritise source-control imaging/procedure where indicated and culture normally sterile intra-abdominal/biliary/abscess material when obtained.
Blood cultures are useful in sepsis; avoid overinterpreting cultures from chronically placed drains.

sourceReconciliation.title: Complicated intra-abdominal infection — source control first
sourceReconciliation.summary: MSIC provides ICU principles while current NAG gives site/severity-specific surgical infection regimens. AbxHub does not convert this into one generic abdominal-sepsis prescription.
points: Current NAG complicated diverticulitis: non-sepsis regimens differ from sepsis/organ-failure regimens; piperacillin/tazobactam is used in the sepsis/organ-failure pathway.
Current NAG specifies extended infusion when piperacillin/tazobactam is administered q8h.
Adequate source control and cultures from normally sterile operative/peritoneal specimens remain central to narrowing therapy.

conditions.name: Complicated Urinary Tract Infection
conditions.summary: HPUSM ASP 2025 gives a simple local empirical regimen for complicated UTI; resistance phenotype should redirect to the dedicated ESBL/AmpC/CRE pathway when present.
before: Obtain urine culture before antibiotics when feasible
Assess obstruction/stones and need for source control
Review previous urine cultures and recent antimicrobials
Check renal function

recommendations.label: Empirical
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefuroxime 750–1500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days

recommendations.label: Complicated UTI
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6–8h OR ampicillin–sulbactam 1.5–3 g IV q6h; may add an aminoglycoside when indicated
alternative: Cefuroxime 750–1500 mg IV q8h
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
Ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days; use site/source and clinical response to individualise.

why: Known ESBL/AmpC/CRE changes the preferred treatment and should not be handled by the uncomplicated empirical card.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Structural/functional urinary abnormalities, devices or systemic illness increase the likelihood of resistant Gram-negative pathogens and failure without source control.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained before antibiotics when systemic/complicated infection is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness and evaluate obstruction, stones, catheter or abscess where relevant.

conditions.name: Congenital Gonococcal Ophthalmitis / Conjunctivitis
conditions.summary: NAG B6 differentiates non-disseminated from disseminated neonatal gonococcal disease.
before: Immediate/frequent saline eye irrigation.
Evaluate for sepsis, arthritis and meningitis; investigate/treat parents and screen for chlamydia/other STIs.

recommendations.label: Non-disseminated
preferred: Cefotaxime 100 mg/kg IV single dose; may continue 48–72 h until systemic infection is excluded.
recommendations.duration: Single dose with possible 48–72 h continuation during systemic evaluation.

recommendations.label: Disseminated
preferred: Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV: q12h if ≤1 week old, q8h if >1 week.
recommendations.duration: 7 days; 10–14 days if meningitis is documented.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Use the syndrome- and pathogen-specific NAG pathway rather than applying a generic antimicrobial regimen.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain appropriate neonatal and maternal STI testing/cultures/NAAT.

conditions.name: Congenital Syphilis
conditions.summary: Congenital syphilis treatment depends on age, evaluation and CSF findings; parenteral penicillin is preferred for proven/probable disease.
before: Perform full congenital-syphilis evaluation according to the current paediatric algorithm, including CSF/long-bone/clinical assessment as indicated.
Evaluate and treat mother/partner(s) and screen for other STIs.

recommendations.label: Birth to first month — proven/probable disease
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg/dose IV: q12h during first 7 days of life, then q8h.
alternative: Procaine penicillin 50,000 units/kg/dose IM q24h.
recommendations.duration: 10 days; NAG notes 14 days when CSF is abnormal.

recommendations.label: Infant considered less likely to have syphilis with normal evaluation
preferred: Benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IM single dose.
recommendations.duration: Single dose when criteria are met.

recommendations.label: Diagnosed after one month of age
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 200,000–300,000 units/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses.
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days.

conditions.name: Congenital Toxoplasmosis
conditions.summary: Congenital toxoplasmosis requires prolonged specialist therapy; NAG lists Fansidar-based and pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine regimens with folinic acid.
before: Paediatric ID/ophthalmology assessment; evaluate CNS and ocular disease.
Confirm availability/regulatory approval of orphan/special-procurement medicines before prescribing.

recommendations.label: Preferred NAG regimen
preferred: Pyrimethamine 1.25 mg/kg/dose + sulfadoxine 25 mg/kg/dose PO every 10 days + folinic acid 50 mg PO every 7 days.
recommendations.duration: 12 months; source notes total duration may extend up to 2 years according to severity/response.

recommendations.label: Alternative regimen
preferred: Pyrimethamine 1 mg/kg/day PO for 2 months then 0.5 mg/kg/day for 10 months + sulfadiazine 100 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses + folinic acid 50 mg weekly.
recommendations.duration: 12 months; may be extended according to severity/response.

conditions.name: Cryptococcal Meningitis
conditions.summary: Induction, consolidation and maintenance phases must be distinguished; HIV/transplant status materially changes the pathway.
before: Confirm host context (HIV/transplant/non-HIV)
Measure and manage CSF opening pressure when appropriate
Check renal, hepatic, haematologic and electrolyte baseline before induction therapy

recommendations.label: Non-HIV / non-transplant — induction
preferred: Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1 mg/kg IV q24h + flucytosine 100 mg/kg/day PO in q6h divided doses
alternative: Use formulation/host-specific specialist regimen when toxicity or access changes the choice
recommendations.duration: Induction generally 4–6 weeks, then consolidation and maintenance phases.

recommendations.label: Consolidation / maintenance
preferred: Fluconazole 400–800 mg PO q24h for consolidation, then 200 mg q24h maintenance
recommendations.duration: Consolidation ~8 weeks; maintenance duration depends on host context.

why: Control of intracranial pressure and phased antifungal therapy are both essential.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Inhaled yeast can disseminate haematogenously to the CNS, especially with impaired cellular immunity; capsular burden and CSF outflow obstruction contribute to raised intracranial pressure.
diagnosticMicrobiology: CSF opening pressure, cryptococcal antigen, microscopy/culture and serum antigen are key; evaluate immune status.

alternative: Use culture/susceptibility to target MRSA or other pathogens when present.
recommendations.duration: Furuncle: 5 days; carbuncle: 7–10 days, with IV→PO switch after source control/clinical response.

recommendations.duration: Response and dissemination assessment determine course; use A5 for disseminated disease.

conditions.name: Cystoisosporiasis (Isospora belli) in HIV
conditions.summary: NAG provides initial treatment and secondary prophylaxis.
before: Assess hydration and persistent diarrhoea.
Optimise ART and immune recovery.

recommendations.label: Initial therapy
preferred: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg IV/PO q6h.
alternative: Pyrimethamine 50–75 mg PO q24h + folinic acid 15 mg q24h OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h.
recommendations.duration: 10 days; extend to 3–4 weeks if symptoms persist.

recommendations.label: Secondary prophylaxis
preferred: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg PO q24h.
alternative: Pyrimethamine 25 mg q24h + folinic acid OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg three times weekly.
recommendations.duration: Continue until immune-recovery criteria in NAG are met (CD4 >200 cells/µL for ≥6 months on ART).

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Use the syndrome- and pathogen-specific NAG pathway rather than applying a generic antimicrobial regimen.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Stool parasitology/NAAT according to availability.

conditions.name: Cytomegalovirus Disease / CMV Retinitis
conditions.summary: CMV end-organ disease requires induction therapy, renal/CBC monitoring and immune-recovery planning; sight-threatening retinitis may need adjunctive intravitreal therapy.
before: Confirm end-organ involvement and immunocompromised context; ophthalmology assessment is urgent for retinitis.
Check baseline renal function and full blood count before ganciclovir/valganciclovir/foscarnet.

recommendations.label: CMV retinitis — systemic induction
preferred: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h for 2–3 weeks
alternative: Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h for 2–3 weeks then 900 mg PO q24h maintenance; foscarnet 60 mg/kg IV q8h or 90 mg/kg IV q12h for ganciclovir toxicity/resistance
recommendations.duration: Induction 2–3 weeks; maintenance may continue until immune recovery criteria are met.

recommendations.label: Extraocular CMV disease
preferred: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h; in CMV oesophagitis/colitis may consider switch to valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h when oral therapy is tolerated
alternative: Foscarnet 60 mg/kg IV q8h or 90 mg/kg IV q12h for treatment-limiting ganciclovir toxicity or resistance
recommendations.duration: 21–42 days or until signs/symptoms resolve, followed by source-specific maintenance where indicated.

why: Intravitreal dosing is ophthalmology-specific and must not be substituted for systemic-dose instructions.
Start/optimise ART and use immune-recovery criteria from the current HIV/OI pathway.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Host immune status, tissue/site involvement, pathogen replication burden, drug penetration and toxicity determine the phase and intensity of anti-infective therapy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Use ophthalmic examination and/or syndrome-appropriate tissue/PCR confirmation where feasible; CMV viraemia alone does not define every end-organ syndrome.

conditions.name: Dacryocystitis / Preseptal Cellulitis
conditions.summary: Treat local lacrimal/preseptal infection and actively exclude orbital cellulitis, abscess and visual compromise.
before: Assess vision, ocular motility, proptosis, pain with eye movement and systemic toxicity.
Urgent imaging/ophthalmology/ENT review if orbital disease is suspected.

recommendations.label: Dacryocystitis
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam 375 mg PO q12h as source-listed oral alternative
recommendations.duration: 7 days.

recommendations.label: Preseptal cellulitis — oral
preferred: Cloxacillin 500–1000 mg PO q6h OR cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h
alternative: Cefuroxime 500 mg PO q12h; clindamycin 300–600 mg PO q8h in allergy; amoxicillin/clavulanate when sinusitis is relevant
recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days, source/response dependent.

why: The current NAG page displays “ampicillin/sulbactam PO 375 mg q12h” for dacryocystitis; verify the locally available oral formulation/product (e.g. sultamicillin-equivalent) before prescribing rather than substituting an IV product orally.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection and host inflammatory response are driven by the anatomical syndrome, pathogen burden, tissue penetration, source control and host factors.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiology specimens when indicated and when this can be done without unsafe delay; use syndrome-specific NAAT/culture where relevant.
Interpret positive results with clinical syndrome, colonisation/contamination risk and prior antimicrobial exposure.

conditions.name: Deep Neck Space Infection / Ludwig Angina
conditions.summary: Deep-neck infection requires airway assessment, cross-sectional imaging/source control and broad oral-flora/anaerobic coverage.
before: Urgent airway assessment and ENT/maxillofacial review.
Image when appropriate and drain a significant abscess.

recommendations.label: Empirical therapy
preferred: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h OR amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h OR cefuroxime 1.5 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h
alternative: Non-severe allergy: cefazolin 2 g IV q8h or ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h + metronidazole; severe allergy: clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days; consider oral switch after a minimum 3–5 days IV when clinically improved and source control is adequate.

conditions.name: Dentoalveolar / Periodontal Abscess
conditions.summary: Source control is definitive; superficial localised abscess in an immunocompetent patient generally does not require systemic antibiotics.
before: Drain/extract/treat the offending tooth.
Assess deep-space spread, systemic signs and immunocompromise.

recommendations.label: Superficial immunocompetent abscess
preferred: No systemic antibiotic; definitive dental source control.
recommendations.duration: No antimicrobial course if adequately localised/source-controlled.

recommendations.label: Deep infection / immunocompromised
preferred: Amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h; may add metronidazole 400 mg PO q8h
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h; allergy: clindamycin 300 mg PO q6h
recommendations.duration: Usually 3–7 days; after successful source control, NAG specifies a minimum 3-day antibiotic course when antibiotics are indicated.

why: Antibiotics without drainage/source control are inadequate for a drainable odontogenic abscess.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection and host inflammatory response are driven by the anatomical syndrome, pathogen burden, tissue penetration, source control and host factors.

conditions.name: Diabetic Foot Infection
conditions.summary: Classify infection severity, obtain deep tissue cultures when needed, and prioritise debridement/off-loading/vascular assessment.
before: Classify mild/moderate/severe infection
Assess osteomyelitis and perfusion
Obtain deep tissue rather than superficial swab when possible
Plan debridement/source control

recommendations.label: Mild
preferred: Cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h
alternative: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h
recommendations.duration: 7–14 days in the local table; adjust to clinical response.

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe
preferred: Ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6h if melioidosis is suspected in the local pathway
recommendations.duration: 7–14 days; deeper infection/osteomyelitis requires its own duration.

recommendations.label: Mild infection
preferred: Cloxacillin 500 mg PO q6h OR cephalexin 1 g PO q12h
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 625 mg PO q8h OR ampicillin/sulbactam (sultamicillin) 375–750 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 1–2 weeks; NAG notes about 10 days following surgical debridement.

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe infection
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
If Pseudomonas suspected: piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h
If MRSA suspected: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h, maximum 2 g/dose; use TDM/renal guidance.
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Skin/soft-tissue involvement: total 2–4 weeks; osteomyelitis requires its own duration pathway.
notes: Do not use antibiotics for an uninfected diabetic foot wound. Local treatment/debridement, off-loading/vascular assessment and culture-guided narrowing remain central.

why: Antibiotics alone do not address ischaemia, necrosis or deep collections.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Organisms breach skin/soft-tissue barriers and trigger local inflammation; deep fascial spread, toxin production, ischemia and impaired host defence drive severe disease.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Superficial swabs are often low yield; obtain deep tissue/pus or operative specimens in severe, necrotising, diabetic-foot or treatment-failure disease.
Blood cultures are appropriate when systemic toxicity, severe immunocompromise or bacteraemia is suspected.

nagDetail.title: Current NAG diabetic-foot severity criteria
points: Mild: at least two local inflammatory findings, erythema >0.5 cm but <2 cm around the wound, and no systemic manifestations/alternative inflammatory explanation.
Moderate: no systemic manifestations but erythema ≥2 cm and/or infection extends deeper than skin/subcutaneous tissue.
Severe: foot infection with systemic manifestations (≥2 SIRS criteria).

conditions.name: Diphtheria
conditions.summary: Suspected respiratory diphtheria is an infection-control and toxin-mediated emergency: give diphtheria antitoxin promptly plus antimicrobial therapy.
before: Isolate and notify/manage with public-health/infection-control pathways.
Do not delay diphtheria antitoxin while awaiting microbiological confirmation when clinical suspicion is high.

recommendations.label: Treatment
preferred: Erythromycin lactobionate 500 mg IV q6h then erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg PO q6h + diphtheria antitoxin
alternative: Benzylpenicillin 25,000 units/kg IV/IM q6h (max 1 million units q6h), then Penicillin V 500 mg PO q6h + antitoxin
OR azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO q24h + antitoxin
recommendations.duration: Antibiotic course 14 days; antitoxin dosing is severity/site dependent.

recommendations.label: Close-contact prophylaxis
preferred: Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM stat
alternative: Erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg PO q6h OR azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h
recommendations.duration: Macrolide prophylaxis 7–10 days per NAG contact pathway.

why: Antibiotics eradicate carriage but do not neutralise circulating toxin; antitoxin remains essential in clinically suspected toxin-mediated disease.

conditions.name: Disseminated / CNS Histoplasmosis
conditions.summary: Severe disseminated and CNS disease require amphotericin-based induction followed by prolonged itraconazole therapy.
before: Assess CNS involvement and disease severity
Check renal/electrolyte/hepatic baseline and major azole interactions

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe disseminated disease
preferred: Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1 mg/kg IV q24h or liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg IV q24h for induction
alternative: Step down to itraconazole after clinical improvement
recommendations.duration: Induction generally about 2 weeks then itraconazole for ≥12 months.

recommendations.label: CNS histoplasmosis
preferred: Liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg IV q24h induction, then itraconazole
recommendations.duration: Prolonged treatment, typically ≥12 months, specialist-directed.

why: CNS disease requires a different intensity/duration from uncomplicated pulmonary disease.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Invasive fungal disease occurs when impaired host defences permit tissue invasion or bloodstream dissemination; organism burden, immune status and anatomic site determine presentation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain site-appropriate fungal microscopy/culture and relevant antigen/molecular tests; identify organism to species where it changes therapy.

conditions.name: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium Complex Infection
conditions.summary: Combination therapy is mandatory to prevent resistance and treat disseminated MAC.
before: Confirm microbiologic diagnosis and HIV/immunocompromised status
Check interaction burden with rifamycins/macrolides

recommendations.label: Disseminated MAC treatment
preferred: Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h + ethambutol 15 mg/kg PO q24h + rifampicin 10 mg/kg PO q24h.
alternative: Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h may replace clarithromycin. NAG may add a fourth drug in severe/high-risk disease: amikacin, streptomycin, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin or moxifloxacin.
recommendations.duration: At least 12 months and until NAG immune-recovery/clinical criteria are met.

recommendations.label: Primary prophylaxis when indicated
preferred: Azithromycin 1250 mg PO once weekly.
alternative: Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h.
recommendations.duration: For NAG-specified CD4 <50 cells/µL context after active MAC/TB are excluded; stop according to ART/CD4 criteria.

why: Macrolide monotherapy rapidly selects resistance.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiological specimens from the suspected source before antibiotics when this can be done without unsafe delay.
Interpret culture/PCR results with syndrome, host factors, prior antimicrobials and colonisation/contamination risk.

conditions.name: Donovanosis (Granuloma Inguinale)
conditions.summary: NAG A13 provides prolonged therapy until complete lesion healing.
before: Evaluate sexual partners and other STI syndromes.

recommendations.label: Donovanosis
preferred: Azithromycin 1 g PO weekly OR 500 mg PO q24h.
alternative: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h OR trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg PO q12h OR erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg PO q6h.
recommendations.duration: At least 3 weeks AND until all lesions have completely healed.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Use the NAG syndrome-, severity-, age- and pathogen-specific branch rather than a generic antimicrobial regimen.

Blood and deep tissue cultures
Assess shock, renal failure and need for ICU support

preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h + metronidazole when required by the source pathway
alternative: Carbapenem-based regimen when MDR/ESBL risk justifies it
recommendations.duration: Continue according to source control, microbiology and clinical response.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Organisms breach skin/soft-tissue barriers and trigger local inflammation; deep fascial spread, toxin production, ischemia and impaired host defence drive severe disease.

conditions.name: Helicobacter pylori Infection
conditions.summary: Use a complete eradication regimen for 14 days and select first- versus second-line therapy according to clarithromycin resistance/exposure, allergy and prior treatment. Do not combine antibiotics ad hoc.
before: Confirm indication for eradication therapy
Review prior macrolide/metronidazole exposure and allergy

recommendations.label: HPUSM 2025 local H. pylori regimen
preferred: Amoxicillin 1 g PO q12h PLUS clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h, with pantoprazole
alternative: Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h PLUS metronidazole 400 mg PO q8h, with pantoprazole
recommendations.duration: 14 days.
notes: Keep this as a dated local-source regimen; current eradication choice should consider resistance history, prior macrolide exposure and the current national/local H. pylori strategy.

recommendations.label: First-line triple therapy
preferred: PPI PO q12h + amoxicillin 1 g PO q12h + clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h
alternative: If antibiotic allergy: PPI PO q12h + clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h + metronidazole 400 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 14 days
notes: NAG recommends clarithromycin-containing first-line therapy where clarithromycin resistance is <15–20%; consider second-line treatment when resistance is >15%.

recommendations.label: Second-line — bismuth quadruple
preferred: PPI PO q12h + tetracycline hydrochloride 500 mg PO q6h + metronidazole 400 mg PO q8h + bismuth subsalicylate 300 mg OR bismuth subcitrate 120–300 mg PO q6h
recommendations.duration: 14 days

recommendations.label: Second-line — fluoroquinolone / PCAB options
preferred: PPI PO q12h + levofloxacin 500 mg PO q24h + amoxicillin 1 g PO q12h
alternative: Potassium-competitive acid blocker PO q12h + amoxicillin 1 g PO q12h + clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 14 days

recommendations.label: Second-line bismuth quadruple therapy
preferred: PPI q12h + tetracycline 500 mg q6h + metronidazole 400 mg q8h + bismuth subsalicylate 300 mg or bismuth subcitrate 120–300 mg q6h.
recommendations.duration: 14 days.

why: Eradication success depends on the complete regimen, acid suppression and resistance pattern.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Persistent gastric colonisation is enabled by urease, motility and mucosal adherence; chronic inflammation contributes to ulcer disease and gastric neoplasia risk.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Use urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy-based testing according to clinical context; account for PPI/antibiotic effects on test sensitivity.

Use the NAG antibiotic-allergy appendix when relevant; confirm prior macrolide/fluoroquinolone exposure and local resistance context.

alternative: Imipenem/cilastatin source-specific severe regimen ± vancomycin
recommendations.duration: Reassess and de-escalate; stop empiric vancomycin after 48 h if no Gram-positive evidence.

conditions.summary: Treat as a syndrome with acquisition timing, MDR risk, respiratory sampling and rapid 48–72 h reassessment. Do not interpret a positive respiratory culture without clinical context.

alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h

preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h ± vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h

recommendations.duration: 7 days

preferred: Cefepime 2 g IV q8h OR piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h
alternative: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h when clinically appropriate
recommendations.duration: 7 days

Do not automatically add MRSA coverage or carbapenem therapy solely because the patient is ventilated; use the source-specific risk criteria and local epidemiology.

conditions.name: Infective Endocarditis

recommendations.label: Native valve — empirical, culture pending
preferred: Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h PLUS gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h PLUS/MINUS cloxacillin 2 g IV q4h
alternative: Penicillin allergy: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h PLUS gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h
recommendations.duration: Source table lists 28–42 days depending on organism; definitive duration must follow organism/valve-specific guidance.

recommendations.label: Prosthetic valve — empirical, culture pending
preferred: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h PLUS gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h PLUS rifampicin 300–450 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: Definitive duration depends on organism and prosthetic-valve context.

recommendations.label: Prosthetic valve <12 months — empirical
preferred: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q12h PLUS gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h PLUS rifampicin 300–450 mg PO q12h
alternative: Optional cefepime 2 g IV q8h OR piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h when non-HACEK Gram-negative coverage is indicated by local epidemiology
recommendations.duration: Narrow promptly to pathogen-specific treatment.

recommendations.label: Native valve — empirical
preferred: Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h; may add cloxacillin 2 g IV q4h when S. aureus is suspected
alternative: Antibiotic allergy: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV q24h
recommendations.duration: Adjust promptly to culture/susceptibility; culture-negative cases warrant ID review.

why: Blood cultures before treatment are central to pathogen-directed therapy.
Aminoglycoside/vancomycin regimens require toxicity monitoring and should be narrowed when cultures permit.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Microorganisms adhere to damaged/prosthetic endocardial surfaces, forming platelet-fibrin vegetations that can seed emboli and metastatic infection.

conditions.name: Melioidosis
conditions.summary: MSIC describes a prolonged two-phase treatment strategy: an IV intensive phase followed by oral eradication therapy, with duration determined by infection site and severity.
before: Obtain cultures; culture is the diagnostic mainstay
Look for deep-seated abscesses and consider CT/ultrasound abdomen/pelvis in culture-positive disease
Assess need for drainage or surgical intervention
Check renal function and TMP-SMX contraindications/interactions

recommendations.label: Initial intensive phase
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h (2 g q8h for CNS infection) OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h
alternative: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6h
recommendations.duration: At least 2 weeks; longer for pneumonia with ICU admission/bacteraemia, deep collections, osteomyelitis, CNS or arterial infection.
notes: Optional TMP-SMX is added in selected sites such as cutaneous disease, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, CNS infection and deep collections in the cited guide.

recommendations.label: Duration framework
preferred: Intensive-phase duration and eradication-phase duration are site-specific; the cited table ranges from 2 to 8 weeks intensive therapy and 3 to 6 months eradication therapy for many listed foci.
recommendations.duration: Use the site-specific melioidosis duration table.

recommendations.label: Intensive phase — mild/moderate non-neurological
preferred: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q6h
alternative: Escalate to a carbapenem regimen for severe disease, persistent bacteraemia or another source-specified indication.
recommendations.duration: At least 14 days IV; site/severity-specific intensive phase may be longer before eradication therapy.

recommendations.label: Severe sepsis / persistent bacteraemia
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem/cilastatin 500 mg IV q6h (higher source-listed dosing may be used for severe infection according to patient/context).
alternative: Once clinically improved, de-escalation to ceftazidime may be considered when appropriate.
recommendations.duration: Intensive phase is prolonged and site/severity dependent; do not shorten below the source-required minimum.

recommendations.label: Neuromelioidosis / ICU septic shock with augmented renal clearance
preferred: Meropenem 2 g IV q8h
alternative: Add trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for selected neurological, osteoarticular, genitourinary/prostatic, skin/soft-tissue, ocular, testicular or pericardial foci according to the NAG pathway.
recommendations.duration: Use the NAG site-specific intensive-phase duration, then complete eradication therapy; ID consultation is strongly appropriate for severe/complex disease.

why: Severe disease, deep infection and CNS/vascular involvement require longer treatment than uncomplicated infection.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Environmental inoculation/inhalation/ingestion can lead to pneumonia, sepsis and multiple deep abscesses; intracellular persistence explains relapse risk and the need for eradication therapy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Culture appropriate specimens (blood plus site-specific samples); alert the laboratory when melioidosis is suspected.

recommendations.label: Stage 1
preferred: Ampicillin 100 mg/kg/dose IV with age-specific interval + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose OR amikacin 15 mg/kg/dose with CGA-specific interval + metronidazole (15 mg/kg load then gestation-specific maintenance)
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam only after recent exposure to first-line antibiotics; PMA-specific interval.
recommendations.duration: Empirical; culture and clinical course guide duration.

recommendations.label: Stage 2 / 3
preferred: Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg/dose IV with age-specific interval + metronidazole neonatal regimen
alternative: Piperacillin–tazobactam only in the source-defined context after recent first-line exposure.
recommendations.duration: NAG lists 10–14 days for the cited Stage 2/3 regimen.

why: NEC is polymicrobial/enteric and treatment includes bowel rest, supportive care and surgical/source-control assessment; antibiotics are only one component.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Prematurity-related intestinal immaturity, dysbiosis, inflammation and mucosal barrier failure can progress to intestinal necrosis and bacterial translocation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Blood cultures are relevant in systemic illness; bowel disease is usually diagnosed clinically/radiographically rather than by a single culture.

conditions.name: Paediatric Community-Acquired Pneumonia — Outpatient / Inpatient / Severe
conditions.summary: Paediatric CAP treatment is setting/severity dependent; viral infection is common, routine macrolide use should be avoided when atypical disease is not suspected, and high-dose amoxicillin is preferred for outpatient bacterial CAP.
before: Assess age, immunisation, oxygenation, hydration, sepsis and complications such as empyema.
Consider influenza antiviral therapy early when clinically suspected and seasonally relevant.

recommendations.label: Outpatient CAP — age ≥3 months
preferred: High-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day PO in 2–3 divided doses (max 1 g/dose; 3 g/day); NAG also provides oral weight-band dosing.
alternative: Standard amoxicillin 45–50 mg/kg/day PO in 3 divided doses only if high-dose is not tolerated.
recommendations.duration: 5 days.

recommendations.label: Inpatient, fully immunised
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 150,000–200,000 units/kg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses.
alternative: Second-line/partially treated: cefuroxime 100–150 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses OR amoxicillin/clavulanate 30 mg/kg/dose IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days.

recommendations.label: Severe CAP / not fully immunised / life-threatening
preferred: Cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses OR ceftriaxone 75–100 mg/kg/day IV in 2 divided doses; may add azithromycin if atypical organisms are being considered.
alternative: Cefuroxime 75–150 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses ± azithromycin.
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days; extend/evaluate complications if not fully recovered.

why: Macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma pneumoniae is common in Asia; avoid routine macrolide use without an atypical indication.

conditions.name: Paediatric Diphtheria
conditions.summary: Paediatric diphtheria is a toxin-mediated/public-health emergency: give antitoxin promptly plus antibiotics to eradicate C. diphtheriae.
before: Immediate isolation/public-health notification and airway/cardiac/neurologic assessment.
Do not delay diphtheria antitoxin while awaiting microbiological confirmation when clinical suspicion is high.

recommendations.label: Treatment
preferred: Diphtheria antitoxin + azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day IV/PO q24h (max 500 mg/dose) OR benzylpenicillin 100,000–150,000 units/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses followed by Penicillin V 50 mg/kg/day PO in 4 divided doses.
alternative: Diphtheria antitoxin + erythromycin 40–50 mg/kg/day IV/PO in 4 divided doses.
recommendations.duration: 14 days total antibacterial therapy.

recommendations.label: Close-contact prophylaxis
preferred: Benzathine penicillin G IM single dose: <30 kg 600,000 units; >30 kg 1.2 million units.
alternative: Erythromycin ethylsuccinate 40–50 mg/kg/day PO q6h OR azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day PO q24h.
recommendations.duration: Macrolide prophylaxis 7–10 days.

conditions.name: Paediatric Hansen Disease (Leprosy)
conditions.summary: Paediatric leprosy requires multidrug therapy and long surveillance; doses differ by age/weight and treatment is specialist/programmatic.
before: Confirm paucibacillary versus multibacillary disease and enrol in specialist/leprosy programme follow-up.
Check weight/age-specific multidrug dosing and monitor treatment toxicity/adherence.

recommendations.label: Age <10 years or <40 kg
preferred: Rifampicin 10 mg/kg PO once monthly + dapsone 2 mg/kg PO daily + clofazimine 100 mg PO once monthly and 50 mg twice weekly.
recommendations.duration: Paucibacillary 6 months (surveillance 5 years); multibacillary 12 months (surveillance 15 years).

recommendations.label: Age 10–14 years and >40 kg

conditions.name: Paediatric Infective Endocarditis / Culture-Negative Endocarditis
conditions.summary: Paediatric endocarditis requires prolonged source- and organism-specific therapy; community-acquired, healthcare-associated, prosthetic-valve and culture-negative pathways differ materially.
before: Obtain multiple blood cultures before antibiotics when this is safe; perform echocardiography and assess embolic/metastatic complications.
Determine native versus prosthetic material, community versus healthcare acquisition and prior antimicrobial exposure.

recommendations.label: Community-acquired empirical IE
preferred: Ampicillin 200–300 mg/kg/day IV/PO in 4–6 divided doses (max 12 g/day) + gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose IV q8h; may add cloxacillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses for acute presentation/MSSA coverage.
recommendations.duration: Definitive duration is organism/valve specific; narrow when cultures are available.

recommendations.label: Healthcare-associated empirical IE
preferred: Vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day IV in 2–3 divided doses + gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose IV q8h; prosthetic-valve context may add rifampicin after 3–5 days according to NAG.
alternative: If epidemiology suggests non-HACEK Gram-negative infection such as Pseudomonas, add cefepime 50 mg/kg/dose IV q8h until cultures are known.
recommendations.duration: Definitive duration is organism/valve specific.

recommendations.label: Viridans streptococci
preferred: Penicillin-susceptible: benzylpenicillin 200,000–300,000 units/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses; ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV in 1–2 divided doses is an alternative.
alternative: For relative penicillin resistance, add gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose IV q8h for 2 weeks to penicillin/ceftriaxone; immediate beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin-based source regimen.
recommendations.duration: 4 weeks native valve; 6 weeks prosthetic valve.

recommendations.label: Enterococcus IE
preferred: Penicillin-susceptible: ampicillin 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses + gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose IV q8h; in source-defined renal impairment/high-level gentamicin-resistance context use ampicillin + ceftriaxone.
alternative: Penicillin-resistant but vancomycin/gentamicin-susceptible: vancomycin + gentamicin.
recommendations.duration: 4–6 weeks depending on symptom duration/native valve; 6 weeks for high-level gentamicin resistance/selected resistant regimens.

recommendations.label: Staphylococcus aureus IE
preferred: MSSA: cloxacillin 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses; MRSA: vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day IV in 2–3 divided doses.
alternative: Cefazolin for non-immediate beta-lactam allergy in MSSA; daptomycin 10 mg/kg IV daily is source-listed for selected MRSA.
recommendations.duration: Usually 4–6 weeks; prosthetic-valve regimens are ≥6 weeks and may include rifampicin plus the source-defined gentamicin course.

recommendations.label: Culture-negative IE
preferred: Ampicillin/sulbactam 300 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses + gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: 4–6 weeks; specialist/microbiology input is recommended, including prolonged incubation when fastidious/fungal causes are suspected.

why: Vancomycin and aminoglycoside exposure require paediatric TDM/renal review; the app should not infer AUC from a single trough.

conditions.name: Paediatric Liver Abscess — Amoebic / Pyogenic
conditions.summary: Differentiate amoebic from pyogenic liver abscess; pyogenic disease usually requires prolonged antibacterial therapy and drainage/source control.
before: Ultrasound/CT to define number, size and drainage requirement.
Obtain blood and aspirate cultures for pyogenic disease; consider epidemiology/serology for amoebic disease.

recommendations.label: Amoebic liver abscess
preferred: Metronidazole 35–50 mg/kg/day PO in 3 divided doses (max 750 mg/dose).
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days.

recommendations.label: Pyogenic liver abscess
preferred: Cefotaxime 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses OR ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV in 1–2 divided doses + metronidazole 22.5–40 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses.
alternative: Piperacillin/tazobactam 300–400 mg/kg/day (piperacillin component) IV in 3–4 divided doses; ESBL-Klebsiella: ertapenem 30 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses in children >3 months.
recommendations.duration: 4–6 weeks; drainage is required in most cases.

why: Amoebic abscess often presents as a solitary lesion; consider drainage when clinically indicated.

conditions.summary: Paediatric lower UTI uses a short oral course chosen with local susceptibility and urine culture when indicated.
before: Obtain urine before antibiotics using age-appropriate collection technique when possible.
Exclude pyelonephritis/systemic illness and investigate recurrent/atypical UTI according to paediatric pathways.

preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 14:1 formulation 80–90 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses OR 7:1 formulation 40–50 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses OR cefuroxime 30 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses.
alternative: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 8–10 mg/kg/day (TMP dose) PO in 2 divided doses OR nitrofurantoin 2 mg/kg/dose q12h sustained-release / 1 mg/kg/dose q6h immediate-release.
recommendations.duration: 3–5 days.

conditions.name: Paediatric Melioidosis
conditions.summary: NAG B12 separates intensive/induction from maintenance/eradication therapy.
before: Obtain cultures and search for deep-seated infection.
Assess neurological, pulmonary, osteoarticular and deep abscess involvement.

recommendations.label: Intensive / induction
preferred: Ceftazidime 200 mg/kg/day IV in 3–4 doses (max 6 g/day).
alternative: Imipenem/cilastatin 75–100 mg/kg/day IV in 4 doses OR meropenem 75 mg/kg/day IV in 3 doses; neurological melioidosis uses higher meropenem dosing per NAG.
recommendations.duration: 2 weeks uncomplicated; 4–8 weeks for complicated pneumonia, deep-seated, neurological, osteomyelitis or septic arthritis.

recommendations.label: Maintenance / eradication
preferred: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP 4–6 mg/kg/dose) PO q12h; add doxycycline in selected high-relapse-risk children >8 years per NAG.
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is the NAG alternative for younger children when needed.
recommendations.duration: Follow NAG site/severity eradication course after induction.

conditions.name: Paediatric Necrotising Fasciitis
conditions.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency; aggressive debridement plus toxin-suppressive combination therapy is essential.
before: Immediate surgical review/debridement; send deep tissue for Gram stain/culture.

preferred: Benzylpenicillin 200,000–300,000 units/kg/day IV in 4–6 divided doses + clindamycin 30–40 mg/kg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses.
recommendations.duration: At least 2 weeks if no deeper focus/heart/bone/joint involvement; source control and clinical course determine final duration.

recommendations.label: Staphylococcal necrotising fasciitis

recommendations.duration: At least 2 weeks if no deeper focus; individualise to debridement and complications.

recommendations.label: Chronic sinusitis / intracranial abscess complication
preferred: Add metronidazole 30 mg/kg/day IV q8h (max 1500 mg/day).
recommendations.duration: Use complication-directed course and source control.

conditions.name: Paediatric Peritonitis
conditions.summary: Paediatric peritonitis management depends on primary versus secondary/nosocomial disease and on prompt source control for perforation or collections.
before: Assess primary versus secondary/perforated-viscus versus nosocomial disease.
Obtain blood/peritoneal cultures and arrange urgent surgical/source-control review for secondary peritonitis.

recommendations.label: Primary / spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
preferred: Cefotaxime 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses.
alternative: Ampicillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day IV q24h; metronidazole can be omitted in primary peritonitis.
recommendations.duration: Individualise; source notes 5 days may be sufficient in immunocompetent mild–moderate disease with source control where applicable.

recommendations.label: Secondary peritonitis — perforated viscus
preferred: Cefotaxime 200–300 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses + metronidazole 15 mg/kg loading then 7.5 mg/kg IV q8h.
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate age/weight-specific IV regimen is source-listed.
recommendations.duration: With adequate source control, short-course therapy may be appropriate; source notes approximately 5 days in immunocompetent mild–moderate disease.

recommendations.label: Secondary nosocomial / ESBL risk
preferred: Piperacillin/tazobactam 300–400 mg/kg/day IV in 3–4 divided doses; culture-proven ESBL: imipenem/cilastatin 60–100 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses OR meropenem 60–120 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses.
recommendations.duration: Individualise to source control and microbiology.

recommendations.label: Systemically unwell
preferred: Cloxacillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses + cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day IV in 3 divided doses OR ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/dose IV q12h.
recommendations.duration: Step down to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate when improving; complete approximately 7 days if no organism dictates otherwise.

recommendations.label: Nodular scabies

recommendations.duration: Age-specific course above.

conditions.name: Paediatric Septic Arthritis / Osteomyelitis
conditions.summary: NAG B8 provides age-stratified empirical therapy and separate duration principles for septic arthritis and osteomyelitis.
before: Obtain CBC, CRP ± ESR and blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible.
Collect synovial fluid/bone specimens if drainage/debridement is performed.
Urgent washout/drainage is important for septic arthritis, particularly the hip.

recommendations.label: Age 0–3 months
preferred: Cloxacillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 doses + cefotaxime 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4 doses.
alternative: Cefazolin may be used as alternative anti-staphylococcal therapy in 1–3 month infants if there is no CNS involvement.
recommendations.duration: SA total 3–4 weeks (4–6 weeks if hip); OM 4–6 weeks; neonatal OM requires at least 4 weeks IV.

recommendations.label: >3 months to 5 years
preferred: Cloxacillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 doses; NAG may add cefuroxime or cefotaxime for age-pathogen coverage.
alternative: Cefazolin 100–150 mg/kg/day IV in 3 doses for suitable suspected S. aureus/S. pyogenes disease.
recommendations.duration: SA 3–4 weeks (4–6 weeks hip); OM 4–6 weeks; oral transition depends on clinical/laboratory improvement and reliable follow-up.

recommendations.label: >5 years
preferred: Cloxacillin 200 mg/kg/day IV in 4–6 doses.
alternative: Cefazolin 100–150 mg/kg/day IV in 3 doses.
recommendations.duration: As above; complex OM may exceed 6 weeks.
