conditions.name: Paediatric Severe / Complicated Malaria
conditions.summary: NAG B12 uses weight-stratified IV artesunate, mandates completion with an oral ACT, and starts broad-spectrum antibiotics concurrently in severe malaria.
before: Treat as an emergency; assess consciousness, glucose, renal/respiratory failure, shock and parasite species.
Start broad-spectrum antibacterial treatment at the same time as antimalarial treatment in severe malaria per NAG.

recommendations.label: IV artesunate — children >20 kg
preferred: Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then 2.4 mg/kg q24h or switch to oral ACT when able.
recommendations.duration: Parenteral artesunate for at least 24 hours (3 doses), then complete a full 3-day oral ACT; NAG treatment framework totals 7 days.

recommendations.label: IV artesunate — children <20 kg
preferred: Artesunate 3.0 mg/kg IV at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then 3.0 mg/kg q24h or switch to oral ACT when able.
recommendations.duration: At least 24 hours/3 parenteral doses, then complete full oral ACT; NAG framework totals 7 days.

recommendations.label: Alternative quinine pathway
preferred: Quinine loading 20 mg/kg IV over 4 hours, then quinine 10 mg/kg IV q8h + doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg/dose PO q12h (max 100 mg/dose) OR clindamycin 10 mg/kg/dose PO q12h.
recommendations.duration: 7 days.

conditions.name: Paediatric Typhoid Fever
conditions.summary: NAG B4 separates empirical, uncomplicated, severe/resistant and chronic-carrier treatment with paediatric doses.
before: Obtain cultures before treatment where feasible and tailor to susceptibility.
Assess severity, complications and chronic carriage.

recommendations.label: Empirical / severe-resistance pathway
preferred: Empirical: ceftriaxone 75–100 mg/kg/day IV q24h (max 2 g/day) for 7–14 days. Severe/suspected resistant: ceftriaxone 80–100 mg/kg/day IV q24h (max 2 g/day) for 7–14 days.
alternative: Severe alternative: ciprofloxacin 30–40 mg/kg/day IV in 2 doses (max 0.8–1.2 g/day) for 7–10 days.
recommendations.duration: 7–14 days according to severity/regimen and clinical response.

recommendations.label: Mild / uncomplicated
preferred: Ciprofloxacin 30–40 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses (max 1.5 g/day) for 5–7 days.
alternative: Azithromycin 20 mg/kg/dose PO q24h (max 1 g/dose) OR susceptible-strain ampicillin.
recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days for ciprofloxacin; source-specific alternatives vary.

recommendations.label: Chronic carrier >1 year

alternative: Ciprofloxacin 20–30 mg/kg/day PO in 2 doses (max 1.5 g/day) OR IV ampicillin when oral therapy cannot be tolerated and isolate is susceptible.
recommendations.duration: 6 weeks for ampicillin/amoxicillin/TMP-SMX; ciprofloxacin 4 weeks.

conditions.name: Paediatric Uncomplicated Malaria — ACT Regimens
conditions.summary: Uncomplicated paediatric malaria is treated with a complete artemisinin-based combination regimen; species determines whether radical cure with primaquine is required.
before: Confirm malaria/species and assess immediately for severe-malaria criteria.
Check G6PD before repeated/high-dose primaquine radical-cure regimens.

recommendations.label: Uncomplicated P. falciparum
preferred: Artemether/lumefantrine: initial dose, second dose 8 h later, then q12h for the next 2 days using NAG weight-band tablets + primaquine 0.25 mg base/kg single dose on day 1
alternative: Artesunate/mefloquine fixed-dose combination q24h for 3 days using NAG weight-band formulation + primaquine 0.25 mg base/kg single dose
recommendations.duration: ACT course 3 days (six-dose artemether/lumefantrine schedule); single-dose primaquine per source regimen.

recommendations.label: P. vivax / P. malariae / P. knowlesi uncomplicated
preferred: ACT (artemether/lumefantrine or artesunate/mefloquine) + primaquine 0.5 mg/kg PO q24h for 14 days for P. vivax
alternative: Quinine 10 mg salt/kg PO q8h for 7 days + primaquine for P. vivax; source also notes selected mefloquine use.
recommendations.duration: Complete ACT/alternative course; P. vivax radical cure 14 days where appropriate.

why: Serve artemether/lumefantrine with a fat-containing food/milk to improve absorption.
NAG cautions against artesunate/mefloquine in children with epilepsy and requires G6PD review before higher/repeated primaquine dosing.

recommendations.duration: Doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days.

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe / inpatient PID

OR clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 3–5 mg/kg IV q24h

alternative: Mild–moderate: clindamycin 600 mg IV/PO q8h + primaquine 30 mg base PO q24h; severe: pentamidine 4 mg/kg/day IV OR clindamycin + primaquine
recommendations.duration: 21 days; severe disease should receive adjunctive corticosteroid according to the NAG regimen.
notes: Consider IV→PO switch after clinical improvement because trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and clindamycin have high oral bioavailability.
Check G6PD status before dapsone or primaquine.

why: High-dose TMP-SMX is weight-based on the trimethoprim component and requires toxicity monitoring.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: P. jirovecii proliferates in alveoli of immunocompromised hosts, producing diffuse interstitial/alveolar inflammation and severe gas-exchange impairment.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Induced sputum or BAL with PCR/microscopy is typical; serum β-D-glucan can support but is not organism-specific.

conditions.name: Postpartum Endometritis
conditions.summary: Treat postpartum uterine infection with broad polymicrobial coverage and reassess for retained products/abscess if response is poor.
before: Obtain cultures when clinically indicated
Assess retained products and source-control need

recommendations.label: Empirical postpartum endometritis
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefotaxime 1 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV once
OR clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h
recommendations.duration: Continue IV until clinically improved (including resolution of fundal tenderness) and afebrile for 24–48 h. If an oral regimen is subsequently administered, NAG lists 14 days total oral-regimen duration.
notes: TDM is required for ongoing gentamicin therapy. Reassess for retained products/abscess or another source if response is poor.

why: Failure to improve should trigger evaluation for retained products, abscess or another diagnosis.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection causes tissue injury through organism-specific invasion/toxin effects and the host inflammatory response; severity depends on pathogen, site, inoculum, source control and host reserve.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiological specimens from the suspected source before antibiotics when this can be done without unsafe delay.

before: Assess for breast abscess or systemic illness.
Support breastfeeding/emptying as clinically appropriate and evaluate nipple trauma/feeding factors.

recommendations.duration: Usually 5–7 days; may extend to 10–14 days if response is poor.

recommendations.duration: Individualise to depth, source control, systemic response and presence of osteomyelitis; consider oral switch when improving.

conditions.name: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes (PPROM) — Antibiotics
conditions.summary: Latency antibiotics after PPROM are source-specific and GBS status affects the regimen.
before: Confirm gestation, membrane rupture, labour/infection status and GBS status.
Do not use a PPROM latency regimen as treatment for established chorioamnionitis.

recommendations.label: PPROM — non-GBS pathway
preferred: Erythromycin ethylsuccinate 400 mg PO q6h OR 800 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days.

recommendations.label: PPROM — GBS-positive pathway
preferred: Ampicillin 2 g IV q6h for 48 h + azithromycin 1 g PO stat on admission, then amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h
recommendations.duration: After the 48-h IV phase, amoxicillin for an additional 5–7 days or until delivery according to the NAG pathway.

conditions.name: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) in HIV
conditions.summary: NAG states there is no effective specific antimicrobial therapy; immune restoration with ART is central.
before: Confirm compatible clinical/neuroimaging picture and specialist diagnosis.

recommendations.label: PML
preferred: No effective pathogen-specific therapy is listed by NAG; optimise effective ART.
recommendations.duration: Clinical course depends on immune restoration; monitor for immune-reconstitution deterioration.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Use the syndrome- and pathogen-specific NAG pathway rather than applying a generic antimicrobial regimen.
diagnosticMicrobiology: JCV testing/neurology-ID evaluation according to clinical context.

conditions.name: Prosthetic Joint Infection
conditions.summary: Do not start routine empirical therapy before adequate cultures in a stable patient; treatment is culture- and surgical-strategy dependent.
before: Withhold empirical antibiotics in stable patient until appropriate specimens are obtained
Define surgical strategy: DAIR vs one-/two-stage revision/removal
Obtain multiple deep tissue cultures

recommendations.label: HPUSM culture-directed retained-implant pathways
preferred: MSSA: cloxacillin 2 g IV q4–6h PLUS rifampicin 300–450 mg PO q12h when the implant remains in situ.
MRSA: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h PLUS rifampicin 300–450 mg PO q12h when the implant remains in situ.
alternative: After the initial IV phase, use an oral combination selected from susceptibility results and the surgical strategy.

Empirical treatment is not recommended before adequate specimens in the stable patient; treatment strategy and duration depend on surgery (no surgery, removal/fusion, DAIR, one-stage or two-stage revision).
recommendations.duration: HPUSM table displays 14–42 days for the initial MSSA/MRSA pathways shown; total strategy remains surgery-, organism- and susceptibility-dependent.
notes: Rifampicin should be included in the cited HPUSM staphylococcal pathway when the implant is retained; do not use rifampicin alone.

recommendations.label: National culture-directed principle
preferred: Empirical treatment is generally not recommended before adequate cultures in stable prosthetic-joint infection.
alternative: For susceptible staphylococci with retained implant, rifampicin-containing combinations are used in source-specific pathways.
recommendations.duration: Typically prolonged and surgery-dependent; check current NAG orthopaedic section.

conditions.diseaseMechanism: Infection reaches bone/joint by haematogenous spread, contiguous extension, trauma/procedure or prosthetic biofilm; devascularised tissue and foreign material reduce antimicrobial efficacy.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain bone/joint/deep tissue or aspirate cultures before definitive antibiotics when clinically safe.
Blood cultures are important for haematogenous disease; imaging defines extent/source-control needs.

conditions.name: Pulpitis / Dry Socket — Antibiotics Not Indicated
conditions.summary: Pulpitis and uncomplicated dry socket require dental/local symptomatic management rather than systemic antibiotics.
before: Confirm there is no spreading infection, deep abscess, immunocompromise or systemic illness.
Provide definitive dental/local treatment and analgesia.

recommendations.label: Pulpitis / uncomplicated dry socket
preferred: No systemic antibiotic. Pulpitis: symptomatic/definitive dental treatment. Dry socket: local saline irrigation, antiseptic/analgesic dressing and pain control.
recommendations.duration: No antimicrobial course.

why: This is an antimicrobial-stewardship condition card: antibiotic exposure is more harmful than helpful when there is no spreading infection.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Anatomical barrier disruption, local microbial invasion and host inflammatory response drive the syndrome; source control is often as important as antimicrobial choice.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain microbiology specimens when indicated and when this can be done without unsafe delay.
Interpret microbiology with the anatomical syndrome, prior antimicrobials and colonisation/contamination risk.

conditions.name: Pyogenic Liver Abscess
conditions.summary: Antimicrobial therapy must be paired with drainage/source control when indicated; sepsis shifts empiric breadth.
before: Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible
Obtain aspirate/drainage culture when procedure performed
Assess abscess size and need for drainage
Assess sepsis/organ failure and prior biliary instrumentation

recommendations.label: HPUSM local liver-abscess table
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h ± metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 14–42 days in the HPUSM table.
notes: HPUSM prints Klebsiella spp., Enterobacteriaceae, Bacteroides, Enterococci, Entamoeba histolytica and “Yersinia E.” among pathogens. Drainage/source control remains essential where indicated.

recommendations.label: Non-sepsis
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ampicillin–sulbactam 3 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefoperazone, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or cefuroxime ± metronidazole according to anaerobic risk
recommendations.duration: 2–6 weeks; shorter with adequate drainage and fever resolution; step down when improving.

recommendations.label: Sepsis / organ failure
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Use source-specific alternatives and resistance-risk assessment
recommendations.duration: 2–6 weeks; source-control dependent. q8h piperacillin–tazobactam is extended over 3–4 h.

recommendations.label: Pyogenic liver abscess
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 1 g IV q12h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h.
alternative: Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: 4–6 weeks.
notes: Consider carbapenem when melioidosis is suspected or there is recent antibiotic exposure.
If Entamoeba histolytica is suspected, add metronidazole 750 mg IV q8h; drainage should be considered.

why: Drainage/source control can shorten therapy and is part of definitive management.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Barrier disruption, obstruction, perforation or infected fluid collections expose normally sterile sites to enteric organisms; source control is a major determinant of cure.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Prioritise source-control imaging/procedure where indicated and culture normally sterile intra-abdominal/biliary/abscess material when obtained.
Blood cultures are useful in sepsis; avoid overinterpreting cultures from chronically placed drains.

conditions.name: Recurrent Urinary Tract Infection — Prophylaxis
conditions.summary: Consider antimicrobial prophylaxis only after behavioural/non-antimicrobial measures fail and after confirming recurrent UTI criteria.
before: Confirm ≥3 UTIs/year or ≥2 within 6 months and verify that episodes were true UTIs.
Address behavioural/personal-hygiene and reversible urological risk factors first.

preferred: Nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg PO ON (macrocrystals) OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO ON (dual-release) OR cephalexin 250 mg PO ON
alternative: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 80/400 mg PO ON OR trimethoprim 100 mg PO ON
recommendations.duration: Continuous prophylaxis 3–12 months OR post-coital single-dose prophylaxis within 2 h of intercourse, with periodic reassessment.

why: Long-term nitrofurantoin has rare pulmonary, hepatic and peripheral-neuropathy toxicity; reassess ongoing need and renal suitability.

conditions.summary: Drainage/source control is central; use broad urinary/systemic coverage initially then tailor to cultures.
before: Urgent urology/radiology source-control assessment for drainage.
Obtain urine, blood and drainage cultures.

preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6–8h OR ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q6h; may add gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h
alternative: Cefuroxime 750–1500 mg IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h; may add gentamicin
recommendations.duration: 2–3 weeks total IV + oral, individualised to extent, drainage/source control, clinical response, imaging and inflammatory markers. Step down after >48 h afebrile/clinical improvement when oral therapy is appropriate.

why: Surgical or pigtail drainage is the mainstay for a drainable collection.

sourceReconciliation.title: Undifferentiated septic shock — local simplified table vs current NAG framework
sourceReconciliation.summary: HPUSM contains a simplified undifferentiated local table stratified by diabetes, whereas current NAG does not use diabetes alone as the principal selector for an empirical sepsis regimen.
points: Current NAG says empirical therapy should be source-directed whenever the source is apparent.

hpusmSepsisBundle.title: HPUSM ASP 2025 sepsis / septic-shock bundle
hpusmSepsisBundle.definition: HPUSM describes sepsis as potentially life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection and septic shock as sepsis with tissue hypoperfusion.
components: Measure lactate; remeasure when initial lactate >2 mmol/L.
Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension OR lactate >4 mmol/L.
Use vasopressor if hypotension persists during/after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP >65 mmHg.
timing: HPUSM states fluid resuscitation and antibiotic therapy should be initiated/completed within 1 hour.
HPUSM states all five bundle components should be completed within 3 hours.
additionalSourceText: HPUSM states at least 60 mL/kg fluid by 6 hours as an adequacy marker and asks clinicians to assess other causes of shock if hypotension persists despite that fluid resuscitation.
Other shock causes listed: bleeding, Addisonian crisis, cardiogenic shock, anaphylaxis and iatrogenic causes (e.g. antihypertensive therapy).
hpusmSepsisBundle.safetyNote: These fluid-volume/timing statements are reproduced as dated HPUSM ASP source content (adapted there from 2018 sepsis literature). AbxHub does not turn the 60 mL/kg/6 h statement into an automatic fluid prescription; use current sepsis/critical-care guidance, dynamic reassessment and patient-specific fluid tolerance.

sourceReconciliation.title: Severe CAP — HPUSM vs MSIC vs current NAG
sourceReconciliation.summary: The three sources agree that severity and Pseudomonas risk matter, but they frame the default severe-CAP regimen differently. AbxHub therefore keeps each regimen separate.
points: Current NAG (Jan 2026-updated severe CAP): amoxicillin/clavulanate is the preferred base regimen; atypical coverage is added when indicated, and antipseudomonal therapy is reserved for Pseudomonas risk.

conditions.summary: Stage-specific penicillin therapy is preferred; neurosyphilis and pregnancy have distinct requirements.
before: Stage disease and assess neurologic/ocular symptoms and pregnancy.

recommendations.duration: Benzathine: 3 weekly doses; procaine: 14 days.

preferred: Aqueous benzylpenicillin 4 million units IV q4h
alternative: Procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM q24h + probenecid; ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM q24h is source-listed for allergy
recommendations.duration: 14 days; severe penicillin-allergy alternatives require specialist assessment.

why: Penicillin is preferred in pregnancy; desensitisation is the standard strategy when a true allergy prevents penicillin use.

preferred: Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1 mg/kg/day IV OR liposomal amphotericin B 3–5 mg/kg/day IV for 2 weeks; then itraconazole 200 mg PO q12h for 10 weeks.
alternative: Voriconazole 6 mg/kg IV q12h on day 1 then 4 mg/kg IV q12h for at least 3 days, OR oral voriconazole if IV unavailable as specified by NAG; then itraconazole 200 mg q12h for 10 weeks.

alternative: Voriconazole 400 mg PO q12h on day 1, then 200 mg PO q12h.
recommendations.duration: Itraconazole at least 8–12 weeks; NAG voriconazole alternative 12 weeks; then maintenance.

alternative: Voriconazole 200 mg PO q12h.
recommendations.duration: Continue until NAG immune-recovery criterion is met (CD4 >100 cells/µL for ≥6 months on ART).

conditions.name: Tetanus
conditions.summary: Management combines wound debridement, toxin neutralisation, antimicrobial therapy and intensive supportive control of spasms/autonomic dysfunction.
before: Immediate wound assessment/debridement
Administer tetanus immune globulin and initiate active immunisation as indicated
Prepare airway/autonomic supportive care for severe disease

recommendations.label: Adult tetanus — antimicrobial + toxin management
preferred: Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6–8h for 7–10 days
PLUS human tetanus immunoglobulin 500 IU IM once
PLUS age-appropriate anti-tetanus toxoid vaccine IM at a different site
alternative: Benzylpenicillin 100,000–200,000 units/kg/day IV divided q6h for 7–10 days, with the same immunoglobulin and active immunisation measures
recommendations.duration: 7–10 days antimicrobial therapy.
notes: Notifiable disease. Wound debridement is essential to eradicate spores/necrotic tissue. IV→PO switch may be considered once clinically improved where an appropriate oral regimen is available.

why: Antibiotics stop bacterial proliferation but do not neutralise toxin already bound to neural tissue.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: C. tetani spores germinate in devitalised anaerobic tissue; tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release, causing rigidity and autonomic instability.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Diagnosis is clinical; culture is insensitive and a negative wound culture does not exclude tetanus.

recommendations.label: HPUSM uncomplicated cystitis
preferred: Nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg PO q6h
alternative: Cephalexin 500 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 3–5 days.
notes: HPUSM lists E. coli, K. pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis in the shared urinary-pathogen block; use current susceptibility/renal-function guidance, especially for nitrofurantoin.

recommendations.label: Uncomplicated cystitis
preferred: Nitrofurantoin or other NAG-listed lower-tract agent based on current local pathway
alternative: Fosfomycin 3 g PO single dose in selected patients; reliability is mainly for E. coli in this context
recommendations.duration: Agent-specific; check latest NAG UTI page.

why: Lower-tract therapy should not be extrapolated to pyelonephritis or systemic infection.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Most bacterial urinary infections ascend from periurethral flora; obstruction, instrumentation, stones and prostate involvement can promote persistence, bacteraemia and sepsis.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained before antibiotics when systemic/complicated infection is suspected.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness and evaluate obstruction, stones, catheter or abscess where relevant.

alternative: Azithromycin 1 g PO stat

conditions.name: Myonecrosis / Gas Gangrene
conditions.summary: NAG A9 treats clostridial myonecrosis as a separate surgical emergency: toxin-suppressing clindamycin is combined with severity-stratified antibacterial therapy and aggressive debridement.
before: Treat as a surgical emergency; obtain urgent surgical review and do not delay aggressive debridement for antibiotic response.
Obtain deep operative tissue/fluid for Gram stain and culture where feasible without delaying source control.

recommendations.label: Mild clostridial myonecrosis
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 4 million units IV q4h PLUS clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: Total 10–28 days, individualized to source control, clinical response and extent of infection.

recommendations.label: Moderate–severe clostridial myonecrosis
preferred: Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h PLUS clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h. If piperacillin/tazobactam is administered q8h, NAG specifies extended infusion over 3–4 hours.
recommendations.duration: Total 10–28 days, individualized to source control, clinical response and extent of infection.

why: Aggressive surgical debridement is necessary to remove all necrotic tissue.

conditions.name: Pertussis Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
conditions.summary: NAG B3 recommends macrolide-based post-exposure prophylaxis for household and specified high-risk close contacts regardless of immunisation status, with age-specific regimens.
before: Confirm meaningful exposure and whether the contact/index context meets NAG PEP criteria.
Assess age, pregnancy, comorbidity, immunisation status and macrolide contraindications/interactions.

recommendations.label: Azithromycin — preferred PEP
preferred: Age <1 month to 5 months: azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day PO q24h for 5 days.
Age ≥6 months: azithromycin 10 mg/kg PO q24h on Day 1 (max 500 mg), then 5 mg/kg PO q24h on Days 2–5 (max 250 mg/day).
recommendations.duration: 5 days.

recommendations.label: Clarithromycin — preferred alternative macrolide
preferred: Age <1 month: not recommended.
Age ≥1 month to 12 years: clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/day PO divided q12h (max 1 g/day).
Age ≥12 years to adult: clarithromycin 1 g/day PO divided q12h.
recommendations.duration: 7 days.

recommendations.label: Erythromycin / TMP-SMX alternatives
preferred: Erythromycin ethylsuccinate (age ≥1 month): 40–50 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses (max 2 g/day).
TMP-SMX (age ≥2 months): trimethoprim component 8 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses (max 320 mg TMP/day).
alternative: For age <1 month, erythromycin is not preferred and should be used only if azithromycin is unavailable.
recommendations.duration: 14 days.

why: NAG identifies azithromycin as the preferred macrolide for PEP/treatment.
PEP is recommended for all household contacts and other qualifying close contacts, including childcare contacts, regardless of immunisation status; use the NAG exposure/high-risk criteria.
Macrolides in very young infants have an association with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, but NAG retains azithromycin because severe-pertussis risk outweighs this potential risk.

Assess severity/complications and recent antibiotic exposure
Check beta-lactam allergy

diagnosticMicrobiology: Routine culture is not usually required in uncomplicated disease; obtain microbiology when there is treatment failure, recurrent/complicated disease or drainage that can be appropriately sampled.

conditions.name: Bacterial Peritonitis — HPUSM Local Table
conditions.summary: HPUSM lists a general bacterial-peritonitis empirical row. Because the source row does not distinguish spontaneous from secondary peritonitis, AbxHub keeps it source-specific and does not merge it into the NAG SBP or complicated intra-abdominal pathways.
before: Define the peritonitis phenotype (spontaneous vs secondary/post-operative)
Assess source control and obtain cultures where appropriate
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis when feasible before antibiotics
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Peritoneal infection may arise through spontaneous translocation or from a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source; subtype and source control materially change management.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Culture ascitic/peritoneal fluid where clinically indicated and obtain operative specimens during source control; interpret results in the context of the peritonitis subtype.

recommendations.label: General bacterial peritonitis row
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days in the HPUSM table.
notes: The HPUSM row does not specify spontaneous versus secondary peritonitis; use the subtype-specific NAG pathway and source-control principles for definitive management.

practicalPathway.title: Practical clinical pathway
assessment: Define peritonitis subtype and source-control need
diagnostics: Obtain source-appropriate cultures when feasible.

regimens.label: General bacterial peritonitis row
regimens.duration: 5–7 days

durationReview.text: 5–7 days

review: Do not use this generic row to bypass subtype-specific NAG/source-control management.
notes: Source-specific local gateway.

conditions.name: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) — HPUSM
conditions.summary: HPUSM Chapter 4 groups UTI/CAUTI by cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated infection and complicated infection with AKI. Culture/source management and catheter necessity remain central.
before: Obtain urine culture before antibiotics when clinically feasible
Assess whether the catheter is still required and replace/remove it according to local CAUTI policy
Assess pyelonephritis, sepsis, obstruction and AKI
Review previous urinary isolates and resistance
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Urinary catheterisation facilitates ascending infection, biofilm formation and bacteriuria; symptoms and systemic features are needed to distinguish infection from asymptomatic colonisation.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain an appropriately collected urine specimen from a freshly replaced catheter/sampling port when treatment is indicated; avoid treating asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria unless a specific indication exists.
Obtain blood cultures in sepsis/systemic illness.

recommendations.label: CAUTI / cystitis
preferred: Nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg PO q6h
alternative: Cephalexin 500 mg PO q12h
recommendations.duration: 5 days in HPUSM Chapter 4.

recommendations.label: CAUTI / pyelonephritis
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h
alternative: Cefuroxime 750 mg IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 7 days in HPUSM Chapter 4.

recommendations.label: CAUTI / complicated
preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h ± aminoglycoside
alternative: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24h ± aminoglycoside
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days in HPUSM Chapter 4.

recommendations.label: CAUTI / complicated + AKI
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam; use the HPUSM Chapter 11 renal-adjustment table.
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days is shown for the complicated-UTI block; individualise to source/response.

practicalPathway.title: Practical clinical pathway
assessment: Confirm symptomatic infection and remove/replace unnecessary catheter
Assess pyelonephritis, sepsis, obstruction and AKI
diagnostics: Collect urine appropriately before treatment when feasible; obtain blood cultures for sepsis.

conditions.name: Hospital-Acquired Infection (HAI) — HPUSM Overview
conditions.summary: HPUSM defines HAI as infection acquired while or soon after receiving healthcare, usually after hospitalisation and manifesting ≥48 hours after admission, with pathogen/resistance patterns that can differ from community infection.
before: Identify the actual syndrome (CLABSI/CRBSI, CAUTI, SSI, HAP/VAP, CDI)
Review prior antimicrobials, length of stay, invasive devices and immune status
Use local microbiology/antibiogram and source-specific cultures
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Healthcare exposure selects for device-associated and antimicrobial-resistant pathogens and changes colonisation pressure and acquisition risk.
diagnosticMicrobiology: Obtain syndrome-appropriate cultures before antibiotics when feasible; distinguish infection from colonisation/contamination and use device/source-control principles.

recommendations.label: HAI syndrome gateway
preferred: Select the syndrome-specific HPUSM/NAG pathway rather than treating “HAI” as a single infection.
alternative: Common HAI syndromes listed by HPUSM: CLABSI/CPI/CRBSI, CAUTI, SSI, HAP, VAP and C. difficile infection.
recommendations.duration: Syndrome-specific.

practicalPathway.title: Practical clinical pathway
assessment: Define the HAI syndrome and device/source-control issue
Review risk factors and local resistance
diagnostics: Use syndrome-appropriate cultures and distinguish colonisation from infection.

regimens.label: HAI syndrome gateway
regimens.duration: Syndrome-specific

durationReview.label: HAI syndrome gateway
durationReview.text: Syndrome-specific

review: Open the specific HAP/VAP, CAUTI, CLABSI/CRBSI, SSI or CDI pathway.
notes: HPUSM Chapter 3 lists Enterobacterales (AmpC/ESBL/KPC/OXA/MBL), non-fermenters, MRSA/VISA/VRSA/MRCONS and enterococcal resistance phenotypes as important HAI contexts.

conditions.name: Adult Tuberculosis — MSIC ICU 2023
conditions.summary: MSIC ICU pathway for drug-susceptible adult tuberculosis, including microbiological confirmation, intensive/continuation phases, body-weight FDCs and steroid indications.
before: Obtain at least two respiratory specimens for AFB smear when pulmonary TB is suspected.
Send mycobacterial culture/susceptibility and Xpert Ultra where available.
Assess extrapulmonary site because duration differs.
Consult Respiratory/ID for relapse, failure, liver failure or HIV co-infection.

recommendations.label: Drug-susceptible TB — intensive phase
preferred: Isoniazid 5 (4–6) mg/kg PO q24h PLUS rifampicin 10 (8–12) mg/kg PO q24h PLUS ethambutol 15 (15–20) mg/kg PO q24h PLUS pyrazinamide 25 (20–30) mg/kg PO q24h.
Pyridoxine 10–30 mg PO q24h; MSIC lists 30 mg/day for patients at high risk of neuropathy.
recommendations.duration: Intensive phase 8 weeks (2 months).
notes: Pulmonary/abdominal/pleural/pericardial/lymph-node TB: total treatment 6 months; bone/joint TB 6–9 months; TB meningitis 12 months in the cited guide.
MSIC includes body-weight FDC tables on book p48/PDF p58.

recommendations.label: Continuation phase
preferred: Isoniazid 5 (4–6) mg/kg PO q24h PLUS rifampicin 10 (8–12) mg/kg PO q24h.
recommendations.duration: Continuation duration depends on site; use the MSIC text above and current TB guideline.
notes: Steroid examples in MSIC: TB meningitis dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day tapered over 6–8 weeks; TB adrenalitis hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h and taper; TB pericarditis prednisolone 60 mg PO q24h tapered over 6–12 weeks.

Xpert Ultra is listed for rapid pulmonary TB detection.
For pleural TB, interpret pleural fluid profile/ADA with low sensitivity of AFB smear/Xpert in pleural fluid.

conditions.name: Severe Acute Pancreatitis — Antimicrobial Decision Pathway
conditions.summary: MSIC states that prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for severe acute pancreatitis or sterile pancreatic necrosis; suspected/proven infected necrosis requires pancreatic-penetrating therapy plus source-control planning.
before: Do not equate fever/systemic inflammation with infected necrosis.
Look for extra-pancreatic infection and evidence of infected necrosis.
Plan drainage/debridement when collections/necrosis fail to respond.

recommendations.label: Sterile severe acute pancreatitis / sterile necrosis
preferred: No prophylactic antimicrobial therapy.
recommendations.duration: Not applicable.
notes: MSIC explicitly states prophylaxis does not reduce morbidity/mortality and should not be used to prevent infection in sterile pancreatic necrosis.

recommendations.label: Suspected/proven infected pancreatic necrosis
preferred: Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8–12h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h.
alternative: Imipenem 500 mg IV q6h OR meropenem 1 g IV q8h.
When multiple invasive-candidiasis risk factors are present: anidulafungin 200 mg day 1 then 100 mg q24h OR caspofungin 70 mg day 1 then 50 mg q24h OR micafungin 100 mg q24h.
recommendations.duration: Guided by repeated clinical and serial radiological assessment.
notes: Percutaneous/endoscopic drainage should be considered for necrosis, peripancreatic collections, pseudocysts or pancreatic abscesses that do not respond.

conditions.name: Biliary Sepsis — ICU Pathway
conditions.summary: MSIC ICU umbrella for acute cholecystitis and acute cholangitis, emphasising early drainage/relief of obstruction plus severity-appropriate antimicrobials.
before: Assess haemodynamic severity and organ dysfunction.
Arrange prompt biliary drainage/relief of obstruction when indicated.
Review previous ERCP/PTC/stents, antibiotics and immunocompromise.

recommendations.label: ICU biliary sepsis
preferred: Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8–12h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h.
alternative: Imipenem 500 mg IV q6h OR meropenem 1 g IV q8h.
recommendations.duration: MSIC table: 7–10 days; shorter 4–7 days after cholecystectomy for perforated/emphysematous/necrotic gallbladder or after source-controlled acute cholangitis.
notes: Consider enterococcal cover in immunocompromised patients, prior endoscopic sphincterotomy and previous antibiotic use.
Drainage/source control remains central.

conditions.name: Parapneumonic Effusion / Empyema — MSIC ICU
conditions.summary: MSIC distinguishes uncomplicated effusion from complicated effusion/empyema using pleural biochemistry and microbiology; complicated disease requires drainage in addition to antimicrobials.
before: Apply Light’s criteria to determine exudate.
Use pleural pH/glucose/LDH, appearance and microbiology to identify complicated effusion/empyema.
Arrange drainage for complicated effusion/empyema.

recommendations.label: Pleural infection management principle
preferred: Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion: antimicrobials.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion: antimicrobials PLUS drainage.
Empyema: antimicrobials PLUS drainage.
recommendations.duration: Prolonged therapy may be required; source control and clinical/radiological response determine duration.
notes: MSIC notes VATS debridement can reduce antibiotic duration and hospital stay in empyema.

organisms.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
notes: Common ICU healthcare-associated pathogen; colonisation is frequent, so infection-vs-colonisation assessment is essential.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental organism that persists on hospital surfaces and equipment; colonises skin/respiratory tract in some patients.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Low intrinsic virulence but strong environmental persistence, biofilm formation and multidrug resistance permit severe infection in vulnerable ICU hosts.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Distinguish colonisation from true infection; CRAB phenotype drives therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus with environmental persistence.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Carbapenem resistance is common in CRAB and often coexists with resistance across multiple antimicrobial classes.

organisms.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
notes: Treatment has an intensive phase and prolonged eradication phase.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Soil and surface water in endemic tropical regions; inoculation, inhalation and ingestion are recognised routes.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Facultative intracellular survival, multiple secretion systems and abscess formation allow latent, relapsing and disseminated melioidosis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment requires intensive and eradication phases; source control and relapse prevention matter.
microbiology.morphology: Slender, motile aerobic Gram-negative bacillus; oxidase positive and able to survive intracellularly.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic resistance to many routine agents; ceftazidime or a carbapenem is used for intensive therapy according to melioidosis guidance, followed by eradication therapy.

notes: Colonisation is common in ICU patients; invasive disease must be distinguished from colonisation.

microbiology.familyOrGroup: Ascomycetous yeasts; family varies by species
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal coloniser of gastrointestinal/skin/mucosal sites; invasive disease follows barrier disruption, broad antibiotics and critical illness.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesion, biofilm formation and host-barrier failure allow candidaemia and deep-seated candidiasis.

microbiology.morphology: Budding yeast; Candida species can form pseudohyphae/hyphae depending on species and conditions.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Species identification and susceptibility matter: non-albicans Candida may have reduced azole susceptibility or intrinsic resistance patterns.

organisms.name: Clostridioides difficile
notes: Antibiotic exposure is a major risk; treatment is severity- and recurrence-specific.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Spores persist in healthcare/community environments; colonises the colon after microbiome disruption.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Toxins A/B damage colonic epithelium and drive inflammation, diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Do not test/treat asymptomatic colonisation; severity and recurrence history determine therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus that produces toxin A/B.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Disease follows microbiome disruption and toxin production; spores persist despite many routine disinfectants, so infection-control measures are critical.

organisms.name: Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (CoNS)
notes: Skin commensals can be contaminants, colonisers or true device-associated pathogens; interpretation depends on clinical context and repeated/paired cultures.

microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive and coagulase negative.
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal skin flora; healthcare-associated infection is strongly linked to intravascular catheters, prosthetic material and biofilm.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesion to foreign material and biofilm formation permit persistence on devices with reduced host clearance and antimicrobial penetration.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Methicillin resistance is common in healthcare-associated CoNS; definitive treatment should follow species/susceptibility and determine whether a positive culture represents contamination or true infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: A single positive culture may be contamination; multiple concordant cultures plus compatible clinical/device findings increase the likelihood of true infection.

organisms.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
notes: Raised intracranial pressure management is central in cryptococcal meningitis.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental encapsulated yeast; infection follows inhalation with later dissemination, especially in impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Polysaccharide capsule and melanin help evade host defences; CNS tropism produces meningitis and raised intracranial pressure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Management includes antifungal phases plus aggressive intracranial-pressure assessment/control.
microbiology.morphology: Encapsulated yeast; India ink may demonstrate the capsule but cryptococcal antigen is more sensitive.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Susceptibility testing is selective; induction therapy is driven by CNS/disseminated disease and host immune status.

organisms.name: Helicobacter pylori
notes: Eradication requires a complete multidrug regimen rather than single-drug therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human gastric colonisation; transmission is mainly person-to-person.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Urease buffers gastric acid; flagella/mucosal adherence and virulence proteins drive chronic gastritis and ulcer/cancer risk.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment should follow current eradication regimens and local macrolide resistance context.
microbiology.morphology: Curved/spiral, motile Gram-negative bacillus; urease positive and adapted to gastric mucus.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Macrolide/metronidazole resistance can cause eradication failure; regimen selection should reflect current local/national guidance and prior macrolide exposure.

resistance.name: AmpC β-Lactamase-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: AmpC risk changes interpretation of β-lactam susceptibility. Site and susceptibility determine whether cefepime or a carbapenem is preferred.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM targeted AmpC pathway
sourceCards.text: HPUSM stratifies inducible AmpC-risk Enterobacterales by UTI severity and severe systemic infection.
bullets: Uncomplicated UTI: nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg PO q6h OR TMP-SMX 15 mg/kg/day (TMP component) in 3–4 divided doses OR single-dose gentamicin; 7 days in the table.
Complicated UTI: TMP-SMX OR once-daily gentamicin OR ceftriaxone 1–2 g q24h for mild disease.
Complicated, moderately severe: cefepime 2 g q8h.
Severe (sepsis > shock/delirium/bacteraemia), normal renal function: cefepime 2 g q8h PLUS gentamicin 5 mg/kg q24h.
Severe with impaired renal function: ertapenem 1 g stat then 500 mg q24h; # requires ID physician approval/authorisation in the HPUSM table.

sourceCards.title: Moderate inducible AmpC risk — urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Uncomplicated cystitis: use a susceptible lower-tract option such as nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX or a single aminoglycoside; pyelonephritis/cUTI: TMP-SMX, once-daily aminoglycoside with TDM, or cefepime are source-listed options.
bullets: Confirm susceptibility before choosing definitive therapy.
Fluoroquinolone is a less-preferred option when susceptible.

sourceCards.title: Outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Cefepime is a key preferred option when susceptible; high-inoculum/severe disease and reduced cefepime susceptibility may shift therapy toward a carbapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam is not recommended for moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organisms in the dedicated consensus.

sourceCards.title: MSIC AmpC-E ICU pathway
sourceCards.text: MSIC warns that Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes and Citrobacter freundii may develop AmpC-mediated resistance during third-generation cephalosporin exposure even when initially susceptible.
bullets: Preferred cefepime 2 g IV q8h; alternative meropenem 1 g IV q8h; cited duration 7 days.
Ertapenem can be considered for targeted therapy once clinically stable with adequate source control.

managementGuide.title: AmpC practical management guide
definition: Moderate-risk inducible AmpC organisms in the MSIDC pathway include Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes and Citrobacter freundii; lower-risk organisms include Serratia marcescens, Providencia spp. and Morganella morganii.

Phenotypic suspicion can involve cefoxitin plus third-generation cephalosporin resistance, but definitive distinction of chromosomal versus acquired AmpC may require genotypic methods; discuss uncertain results with clinical microbiology.

siteRows.preferred: Susceptible nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX or a single gentamicin/amikacin dose
siteRows.alternative: Ciprofloxacin if susceptible; if already improving on a susceptible empirical beta-lactam, count that exposure and prefer oral step-down when feasible.

siteRows.preferred: TMP-SMX, once-daily gentamicin/amikacin with TDM, or cefepime when susceptible
siteRows.alternative: Ciprofloxacin is less preferred when susceptible.

siteRows.preferred: Cefepime when susceptible
siteRows.alternative: For cefepime SDD/high-burden disease, cefepime or a carbapenem may be used per source context; carbapenem is preferred for high-burden disease and cefepime-resistant infection. Seek ID/microbiology input when cefepime non-susceptible.

siteRows.preferred: Non-severe disease: treat according to susceptibility. Severe/high-burden disease: cefepime is preferred in the MSIDC pathway.
siteRows.alternative: Escalate/seek specialist input when cefepime is non-susceptible.

dosing: MSIDC adult appendix: cefepime 2 g IV q8h for non-cystitis infection; prolonged infusion over 3–4 h is recommended for severe/high-burden disease or susceptible-dose-dependent isolates.
Meropenem adult appendix: 1 g IV q8h for non-CNS AmpC/ESBL infection; 2 g IV q8h for CNS infection, with prolonged infusion in the source strategy.
pearls: Avoid piperacillin–tazobactam for moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC Enterobacterales in the dedicated MSIDC guidance.
Reserve newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations for difficult-to-treat carbapenem-resistant infection rather than routine AmpC treatment.
managementGuide.duration: AmpC status does not set duration by itself. Use the syndrome/source-control duration for the actual infection and include effective empirical therapy in the total course when the source allows completion.
ipc: Standard precautions; escalate infection-control measures according to institutional epidemiology and MDRO policy.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
resistance.summary: CRAB treatment starts with infection-versus-colonisation assessment, then uses severity, ampicillin-sulbactam susceptibility, infection site and full susceptibility data. Malaysian HPUSM/MSIDC guidance places high-dose sulbactam-based therapy at the centre of many true-infection regimens.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM CRAB — severity and susceptibility stratification
sourceCards.text: Local targeted guidance separates mild infection from moderate–severe disease and also distinguishes ampicillin-sulbactam susceptible versus non-susceptible mild CRAB.
bullets: Mild + susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV q4h.
Mild + non-susceptible: high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam 9 g IV q8h.
Moderate–severe: ampicillin/sulbactam 9 g IV q8h infused over 3 h, with or without meropenem 2 g IV q8h infused over 3 h according to the local pathway/authorisation requirements.
Local table duration: 7–10 days; individualise by site, source control and response.

sourceCards.title: MSIDC CRAB — core treatment principles
sourceCards.text: Do not treat colonisation. For true CRAB infection, MSIDC uses sulbactam-based therapy with dose intensity and combination strategy determined by severity and susceptibility.
bullets: Mild + ampicillin-sulbactam susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam providing 6 g sulbactam/day may be used as monotherapy.

Mild + non-susceptible: ampicillin/sulbactam providing 9 g sulbactam/day plus minocycline or polymyxin B; colistin may be used if polymyxin B is unavailable and is preferred for UTI because of urinary exposure.
Moderate–severe: combination therapy centred on ampicillin/sulbactam providing 9 g sulbactam/day plus minocycline or polymyxin B.
Minocycline has low serum/urinary concentrations; site matters.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM sulbactam preparation / renal table
sourceCards.text: The local appendix gives practical formulation, renal/RRT, dilution and infusion instructions for high-dose sulbactam regimens.
bullets: Unasyn 1.5 g/vial contains ampicillin 1 g + sulbactam 0.5 g (1:0.5).
Sulperazone 1 g/vial contains cefoperazone 500 mg + sulbactam 500 mg (1:1).
Target sulbactam/day in the local table: CrCl >50: 9 g/day; CrCl 20–50: 6 g/day; CrCl <20/HD: 4 g/day; CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF: 9 g/day.
Dilute in 100 mL; compatible diluents listed locally include water for injection, 0.9% sodium chloride and 5% dextrose; infuse over 4 h.

sourceCards.title: MSIDC CRAB — companion agents / cautions
sourceCards.text: The dedicated MDR guideline adds site-specific polymyxin considerations and cautions against several low-value combinations.
bullets: Polymyxin B is generally preferred over colistin outside UTI; colistin is preferred for UTI because CMS renal elimination can produce higher urinary exposure.
Cefiderocol may be considered for CRAB, preferably combined with high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam in the cited guidance.
Nebulised antibiotics are not routinely recommended for CRAB.
Meropenem + colistin has not demonstrated superiority to colistin monotherapy in cited trials; avoid routine triple meropenem + polymyxin + ampicillin/sulbactam because of toxicity/limited benefit.

sulbactamGuide.title: Dosage regimen of sulbactam for Acinetobacter MDR
formulations: Unasyn 1.5 g/vial = ampicillin 1 g + sulbactam 0.5 g (ratio 1:0.5).
Sulperazone 1 g/vial = cefoperazone 500 mg + sulbactam 500 mg (ratio 1:1).
administration: Listed compatible diluents: water for injection, 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose.
precautions: High-dose Unasyn can produce substantial sodium exposure; the local guide gives an example of 9 g q8h providing about 90 mmol sodium/day. Monitor for hypernatraemia and excess sodium/fluid load; monitor sodium/fluid balance and consider a lower-sodium diluent strategy where appropriate and compatible.

High-dose cefoperazone/sulbactam may contribute to vitamin-K deficiency/hypoprothrombinaemia; monitor haematologic/coagulation parameters where clinically indicated and follow local specialist/pharmacy guidance.

HPUSM page 22 states that exogenous IV vitamin K 10 mg once daily may be administered while on IV cefoperazone/sulbactam. AbxHub preserves this as source wording only; do not treat it as universal prophylaxis—verify current pharmacy/ID practice and bleeding/coagulation risk.

HPUSM page 22 notes Unasyn 1.5 g/vial contains about 5 mmol sodium and gives 9 g q8h as an example providing about 90 mmol sodium/day; monitor sodium/fluid burden. It also lists 0.18% sodium chloride + 4.25% dextrose (QSD1) or 5% dextrose as lower-sodium diluent options where appropriate.

managementGuide.title: CRAB practical management guide
definition: First distinguish true CRAB infection from colonisation; then stratify severity, ampicillin-sulbactam susceptibility, infection site and full AST.
High-dose sulbactam exposure is the backbone of the HPUSM/MSIDC pathways; use the dedicated sulbactam table below for formulation, renal/RRT and infusion details.

siteRows.preferred: Ampicillin-sulbactam using the source-defined susceptible regimen.
siteRows.alternative: Use the dedicated source cards and sulbactam table below.

siteRows.preferred: High-dose sulbactam-based therapy, with a susceptibility/site-directed companion according to the HPUSM/MSIDC pathway.
siteRows.alternative: Minocycline or polymyxin B are common source-listed companions; colistin is preferred over polymyxin B for urinary-source infection if a polymyxin is required.

dosing: Use the dedicated Dosage regimen of sulbactam for Acinetobacter MDR table on this page; it contains formulation ratios, CrCl/RRT targets, 100-mL dilution and four-hour infusion instructions.
pearls: Minocycline has low serum/urinary concentrations; site matters.
Avoid routine nebulised antibiotic therapy and low-value/toxic combinations where the dedicated source advises against them.
managementGuide.duration: HPUSM local table gives 7–10 days for the CRAB regimen shown; individualise by infection site, source control and response.
ipc: Apply CRAB/contact precautions according to local infection-control policy.

sourceReconciliation.title: HPUSM internal sulbactam infusion-duration difference
sourceReconciliation.summary: HPUSM Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 print different infusion durations for the high-dose ampicillin–sulbactam CRAB regimen.
points: Chapter 9 page 21: ampicillin–sulbactam 9 g q8h over 3 h for moderate–severe CRAB.
Chapter 10 page 22: high-dose sulbactam preparations are administered over 4 h.
AbxHub preserves both source statements and does not choose one automatically; verify the current HPUSM ID/pharmacy protocol.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: CRE is heterogeneous. Determine whether carbapenemase is present and identify the enzyme (e.g. NDM/MBL, KPC, OXA-48-like) because this can change active options.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM targeted CRE pathway
sourceCards.text: HPUSM stratifies CRE by urinary vs extra-urinary site and severity; several severe-regimen agents are restricted/ID-authorised locally.
bullets: Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO q6h OR single-dose aminoglycoside.
Complicated cystitis: TMP-SMX 15 mg/kg/day (TMP component) in 3–4 divided doses OR ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg PO q12h.
Outside UTI, mild–moderate: TMP-SMX 15 mg/kg/day (TMP component) in 3–4 divided doses OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q8h.
Severe: meropenem 2 g IV q8h (source prints “infusion”) PLUS gentamicin 7 mg/kg q24h, OR polymyxin B 12,500 IU/kg q12h, OR tigecycline 100 mg q12h; 7–10 days in the table.
# in HPUSM denotes ID physician approval/authorisation.

sourceCards.title: Non-CP CRE with retained meropenem/imipenem susceptibility
sourceCards.text: Use high-dose meropenem or imipenem with 3–4 h extended infusion when the source MIC criteria are satisfied.

sourceCards.title: CRE outside urinary tract — ceftazidime/avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Ceftazidime–avibactam is preferred. Cefiderocol, high-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B are less-preferred source-listed alternatives; combination strategies are reserved for selected severe/high-burden scenarios.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM
sourceCards.text: Preferred: ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam administered simultaneously, OR cefiderocol.
bullets: Consider high-dose extended-infusion meropenem as a companion only when MIC ≤8 mg/L in the source-defined combination context.

sourceCards.title: MSIC CRE definition / Malaysian ICU context
sourceCards.text: MSIC defines CRE as Enterobacterales resistant to at least one carbapenem (or carbapenemase-producing) and highlights NDM-1 and OXA-48 as common Malaysian variants.
bullets: Risk factors include comorbidity, prior antimicrobials, devices, prolonged ICU/hospital stay and MDR co-colonisation.
Source regimen: colistin or polymyxin B; alternative ceftazidime/avibactam plus aztreonam for NDM context in the cited table.
Colistin is preferred over polymyxin B for urinary infection in the source.

managementGuide.title: CRE / CPE practical management guide
definition: CRE is heterogeneous: separate carbapenemase-producing CRE from non-carbapenemase CRE and, when possible, identify the enzyme (e.g. NDM/MBL, OXA-48-like, KPC) because this changes active beta-lactam options.

Intrinsic imipenem elevation in Proteus/Morganella/Providencia must not be mislabelled as CRE without interpreting the other carbapenems. Carbapenemase testing may use phenotypic or molecular methods according to laboratory capability.

siteRows.site: Non-CP CRE · meropenem/imipenem MIC ≤1 µg/mL, ertapenem non-susceptible
siteRows.preferred: High-dose meropenem or imipenem using 3–4 h extended infusion.
siteRows.alternative: Use the renal/RRT tool after selecting the source-defined clinical dose.

siteRows.site: CRE non-susceptible to all carbapenems · uncomplicated cystitis
siteRows.preferred: Susceptible nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX
siteRows.alternative: Fosfomycin for E. coli only, ciprofloxacin or a single aminoglycoside dose.

siteRows.preferred: Susceptible TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime-avibactam or cefiderocol
siteRows.alternative: Once-daily aminoglycoside with TDM or colistin; urinary-source polymyxin choice differs from non-urinary infection.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftazidime-avibactam
siteRows.alternative: Cefiderocol, high-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B are less preferred. In moderate–severe/high-burden disease, MSIDC favours an additional susceptible companion when cefiderocol/tigecycline/polymyxin is used.

siteRows.site: Outside urinary tract · ceftazidime-avibactam resistant, presumed/confirmed NDM
siteRows.preferred: Ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam administered simultaneously, or cefiderocol
siteRows.alternative: High-dose tigecycline (avoid for bacteraemia) or polymyxin B are less preferred; selected severe/high-burden cases may require susceptibility-directed combination therapy.

siteRows.site: Outside urinary tract · ceftazidime-avibactam resistant, mechanism unknown
siteRows.preferred: Cefiderocol in the source algorithm
siteRows.alternative: High-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B; obtain ID/clinical microbiology input and define the carbapenemase when possible.

dosing: Ceftazidime-avibactam: MSIDC adult appendix lists 2.5 g IV q8h over 3 h in normal renal function; renal adjustment is required.
Aztreonam: 2 g IV q6–8h over 3 h in the adult appendix when used with ceftazidime-avibactam for CRE; the treatment section specifies simultaneous administration and notes Y-site compatibility.
Tigecycline high-dose strategy: 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg q12h; avoid relying on tigecycline for bloodstream/intravascular-source infection because serum concentrations are low.
Polymyxin B: 2.0–2.5 mg/kg IV loading, then 1.25–1.5 mg/kg q12h in the MSIDC adult appendix; no renal dose adjustment is listed there, but toxicity monitoring remains essential.
Colistin: adult appendix uses a 9-MU loading strategy with renal-adjusted maintenance; prefer colistin rather than polymyxin B for urinary-source infection when a polymyxin is required.
pearls: If meropenem MIC ≤8 mg/L, the MSIDC severe/high-burden combination framework may include the highest-dose prolonged-infusion meropenem as a companion; this is not carbapenem monotherapy for fully resistant CRE.
Polymyxins have more toxicity and generally worse outcome data than newer active beta-lactam options; do not default to them when a preferred active agent is available.
Cefiderocol is usually used as monotherapy in the cited literature, although emerging NDM-associated resistance is noted; specialist input is appropriate for severe disease.
managementGuide.duration: CRE phenotype does not determine duration. Use the diagnosed syndrome, source control and response; document a review/stop date and reassess combination therapy as soon as clinically appropriate.
ipc: Treat infection, not colonisation. CP-CRE generally warrants more intensive infection-control attention than non-CP CRE; follow local screening/contact-precaution policy.

resistance.name: ESBL-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase phenotype. Treatment depends on infection site, severity and susceptibility; avoid treating the resistance label without the clinical syndrome.

sourceCards.title: Local severe/critical illness signal
sourceCards.text: HPUSM uses ertapenem for selected severe ESBL infection and meropenem/imipenem for critically ill/intubated ICU patients; hypoalbuminaemia and infection site alter the choice.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM targeted ESBL-E pathway
sourceCards.text: HPUSM separates mild/uncomplicated urinary infection, non-severe extra-urinary infection, severe SIRS+ infection and critical illness.
bullets: Mild/uncomplicated UTI: TMP-SMX 15 mg/kg/day (TMP component) in 3–4 divided doses OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg q6h; 7 days.
Non-severe outside UTI: amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h; 7 days.
Severe/SIRS+: ertapenem 1 g q24h; in hypoalbuminaemia HPUSM prints ertapenem 1 g q12h; 7–10 days and # ID authorisation.
Critically ill/intubated/ICU: meropenem or imipenem; 7–10 days and # ID authorisation.
If cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam was started empirically for cystitis caused by ESBL-E and clinical improvement occurs, HPUSM states no change or extension is necessary.

sourceCards.title: Uncomplicated cystitis / pyelonephritis-cUTI
sourceCards.text: Use susceptible oral/lower-tract options for uncomplicated cystitis; for pyelonephritis/cUTI, TMP-SMX or ciprofloxacin are preferred when susceptible, with aminoglycoside/carbapenem alternatives in selected cases.
bullets: Avoid unnecessary carbapenem exposure when a reliable active narrower option exists.

sourceCards.title: Infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Carbapenem is the preferred class in the dedicated MSIDC guidance; in critically ill patients or marked hypoalbuminaemia, meropenem/imipenem is favoured over ertapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam and cefepime are not recommended as definitive ESBL therapy outside narrow exceptions described in the source.

sourceCards.title: Current NAG organism quick guide — ESBL Enterobacterales
sourceCards.text: Current NAG quick guide lists ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem as preferred agents for ESBL Enterobacterales. Use the MSIDC site-specific pathway above/below to avoid unnecessary carbapenem exposure when a reliable narrower option is appropriate.
bullets: The NAG quick guide is a rapid organism reference; definitive therapy still requires syndrome, severity and susceptibility context.

managementGuide.title: ESBL practical management guide
definition: ESBL enzymes hydrolyse penicillins, expanded-spectrum cephalosporins and monobactams but not carbapenems/cephamycins; treatment still depends on site, severity and reliable susceptibility testing.
Current NAG organism quick guide lists ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem as preferred agents for ESBL Enterobacterales; the dedicated MSIDC pathway provides the site-specific narrower options below.

siteRows.preferred: Nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX when susceptible
siteRows.alternative: Ciprofloxacin, one aminoglycoside dose, fosfomycin for E. coli only, or ertapenem if no suitable option.

siteRows.preferred: TMP-SMX or ciprofloxacin when susceptible
siteRows.alternative: Once-daily aminoglycoside with TDM, or ertapenem/meropenem/imipenem when no suitable narrower option.

siteRows.preferred: Carbapenem therapy in the dedicated MSIDC pathway
siteRows.alternative: In critical illness or marked hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), favour meropenem or imipenem rather than ertapenem.

siteRows.preferred: Use the local HPUSM ESBL pathway and patient severity; critically ill/intubated ICU patients are directed toward meropenem/imipenem rather than ertapenem.
siteRows.alternative: Reassess de-escalation once microbiology and clinical response are known.

dosing: MSIDC adult appendix: meropenem 1 g IV q8h for non-CNS ESBL/AmpC infection; 2 g IV q8h for CNS infection with prolonged infusion strategy where specified.
Ertapenem adult appendix: 1 g IV q24h in normal renal function; do not use ertapenem for Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Acinetobacter or CNS infection.
pearls: MSIDC does not recommend piperacillin–tazobactam as definitive ESBL therapy regardless of reported susceptibility, except it allows completion in a narrow uncomplicated-cystitis scenario when already improving and no oral step-down is available.
MSIDC likewise does not recommend cefepime as definitive ESBL therapy regardless of susceptibility, with the same narrow cystitis-completion exception.
managementGuide.duration: Use the duration for the diagnosed syndrome and source control; ESBL phenotype alone does not justify a longer course.
ipc: Apply MDRO precautions/risk assessment according to local infection-prevention policy; colonisation should not be treated as infection.

resistance.name: KPC-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Carbapenemase-producing CRE with a serine carbapenemase mechanism. Therapy should be susceptibility- and site-directed using dedicated CRE guidance.

sourceCards.title: If ceftazidime–avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: For CRE infection outside the urinary tract, MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam as the preferred option when susceptible.
bullets: Confirm susceptibility and infection site.
Use ID/clinical microbiology review for severe/high-burden infection.

managementGuide.title: KPC-producing CRE guide
definition: KPC is a serine carbapenemase. Ceftazidime-avibactam activity must be confirmed by susceptibility testing; do not infer susceptibility from the enzyme name alone.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftazidime-avibactam
siteRows.alternative: Cefiderocol, high-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B are less preferred in the MSIDC pathway; use the full CRE severity/combination framework for high-burden disease.

dosing: Ceftazidime-avibactam: 2.5 g IV q8h over 3 h in the MSIDC adult normal-renal table; renal adjustment is required.
pearls: Obtain mechanism plus AST rather than treating all CP-CRE identically.
managementGuide.duration: Use the infection-syndrome duration and source-control plan.
ipc: Manage as CP-CRE according to local infection-control policy.

resistance.name: MDR / DTR Pseudomonas aeruginosa
resistance.summary: Use site, severity and in-vitro activity. DTR Pseudomonas should trigger dedicated MDR guidance rather than automatic carbapenem escalation.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM MDR/XDR/DTR Pseudomonas targeted pathway
sourceCards.text: HPUSM uses a severity/site-stratified pathway that includes gentamicin and ceftolozane–tazobactam.
bullets: Cystitis: gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV single dose (stat).
Mild–moderate: gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg daily OR ceftolozane–tazobactam 3 g IV q8h AND/OR any in-vitro active susceptible agent; 7 days.
Severe: gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg daily PLUS ceftolozane–tazobactam 3 g IV q8h, OR any in-vitro active susceptible agent; 7–10 days.

Important source difference: the dedicated MSIDC MDR guideline shown elsewhere in AbxHub cautions that IV gentamicin is not recommended for Pseudomonas in its pathway because CLSI breakpoints are unavailable. Do not silently merge the two sources.

sourceCards.title: MDR Pseudomonas, carbapenem non-susceptible but traditional β-lactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Prefer susceptible ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam using high-dose extended infusion.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — cystitis / cUTI
sourceCards.text: Preferred newer β-lactams are ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam when susceptible; site-specific alternatives include amikacin, colistin or cefiderocol.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Prefer ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam. Cefiderocol or polymyxin B + a second susceptible agent are less-preferred source options.
bullets: MSIDC does not recommend routine combination therapy when an optimal active agent is available.
Nebulised antibiotics are not recommended in the cited respiratory DTR-Pseudomonas guidance.

sourceCards.title: MSIC difficult-to-treat Pseudomonas
sourceCards.text: MSIC defines DTR P. aeruginosa by non-susceptibility to piperacillin/tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem, imipenem/cilastatin, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.
bullets: Source options include colistin or polymyxin B; alternatives ceftolozane/tazobactam 1.5–3 g q8h or ceftazidime/avibactam 2.5 g q8h.
Higher ceftolozane/tazobactam dose is required in HAP/VAP in the source.

managementGuide.title: MDR / DTR Pseudomonas practical guide
definition: MDR P. aeruginosa can remain susceptible to traditional non-carbapenem beta-lactams despite carbapenem non-susceptibility; DTR phenotype requires the dedicated newer-agent pathway and isolate-specific AST.

siteRows.site: MDR · carbapenem non-susceptible but ceftazidime/cefepime/pip-tazo susceptible
siteRows.preferred: Use the active traditional beta-lactam at high dose with extended infusion: ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam.
siteRows.alternative: Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin are less preferred if susceptible.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam
siteRows.alternative: Single-dose amikacin, colistin or cefiderocol. Avoid oral fosfomycin for Pseudomonas.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam
siteRows.alternative: Once-daily amikacin with TDM, colistin or cefiderocol; use colistin rather than polymyxin B for urinary-source infection if a polymyxin is required.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam
siteRows.alternative: Cefiderocol or polymyxin B plus a second susceptible agent when no better active option; ID/microbiology review if no susceptible companion exists.

dosing: Piperacillin-tazobactam for MDR Pseudomonas: 4.5 g IV q6h; source appendix supports high-dose extended infusion (maintenance over about 4 h after a loading dose).
Ceftazidime: 2 g IV q6–8h; prolonged infusion over 4 h is recommended for severe/high-burden disease.
Cefepime: 2 g IV q8h for non-cystitis infection; prolonged infusion over 3–4 h is recommended for severe/high-burden disease.
Ceftolozane-tazobactam: 1.5 g IV q8h for cystitis; 3 g IV q8h for other infection, with 3-h extended infusion potentially needed in severe DTR disease.
Ceftazidime-avibactam: 2.5 g IV q8h over 3 h.
Cefiderocol: 2 g IV q8h in the adult normal-renal appendix; use renal/augmented-clearance adjustments from the source table.
pearls: Reserve newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor agents for DTR Pseudomonas rather than using them routinely when a traditional active beta-lactam remains suitable.
MSIDC does not recommend nebulised antibiotics for DTR Pseudomonas respiratory infection.
IV gentamicin is not recommended for Pseudomonas in the cited MSIDC document because CLSI breakpoints are unavailable.
Routine combination therapy is not recommended when an optimal active agent is available because benefit is unproven and adverse effects increase.
managementGuide.duration: Use the diagnosed infection-site duration (e.g. pneumonia, cUTI, bloodstream infection) and clinical/source-control response; DTR phenotype alone does not mandate a longer course.
ipc: Apply MDRO/contact precautions according to local DTR-Pseudomonas policy and institutional epidemiology.
