resistance.name: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: MRSA is resistant to usual antistaphylococcal β-lactams because of altered PBP2a. Use local MRSA risk/prevalence and syndrome severity to decide empirical coverage.

sourceCards.title: Local guidance
sourceCards.text: HPUSM recommends vancomycin for empirical therapy when MRSA risk is high/severe and for confirmed MRSA; it states vancomycin is inferior to cloxacillin for MSSA.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM MRSA risk / infection-control context
sourceCards.text: HPUSM lists indwelling catheter, ICU admission, prolonged hospitalisation, multiple comorbidities and severe underlying disease as MRSA risk factors and recommends meticulous hand hygiene/contact precautions.
bullets: The guide cites a historical HPUSM MRSA infection-rate publication from 2002–2007; AbxHub labels that figure as historical and does not use it as a current antibiogram/prevalence estimate.
Vancomycin is source-listed for high MRSA risk/severe disease and confirmed MRSA; de-escalate to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam when MSSA is confirmed and clinically appropriate.

managementGuide.title: MRSA practical guide
definition: Methicillin resistance predicts resistance to usual anti-staphylococcal beta-lactams; current NAG notes ceftaroline as the beta-lactam exception in its quick guide. Confirm vancomycin MIC/susceptibility rather than assuming activity.

siteRows.site: Confirmed / high-risk MRSA where systemic therapy is required
siteRows.preferred: Vancomycin is the principal IV option in HPUSM/NAG quick guidance.
siteRows.alternative: NAG quick guide lists linezolid and ceftaroline as IV alternatives; oral/CA-MRSA options are syndrome- and susceptibility-dependent.

dosing: Use the vancomycin TDM workflow for loading, renal/RRT and exposure monitoring rather than a fixed trough-only approach.
pearls: Rifampicin should not be used alone for staphylococcal antimicrobial therapy.
When the isolate is MSSA, de-escalate from vancomycin to an effective anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam unless contraindicated.
managementGuide.duration: Duration depends on syndrome and whether disease is complicated (e.g. bacteraemia/endocarditis/deep focus) rather than the MRSA phenotype alone.
ipc: Follow local MRSA infection-control policy and distinguish colonisation from infection.

resistance.name: Methicillin-Susceptible Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: HPUSM notes MSSA causes community and hospital-acquired bloodstream/invasive infection and that vancomycin is inferior to anti-staphylococcal penicillins such as cloxacillin for MSSA.

sourceCards.title: Local HPUSM principle
sourceCards.text: Use an anti-staphylococcal penicillin such as cloxacillin for susceptible S. aureus rather than continuing vancomycin solely for convenience; complicated MSSA infection warrants ID consultation.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM complicated MSSA — ID consultation triggers
sourceCards.text: HPUSM advises infectious-disease consultation for complicated MSSA infection.
bullets: Endocarditis.
Prosthetic-device involvement.
Infection involving ≥2 organs/systems (disseminated infection).
Positive blood culture >72 h after effective antibiotic initiation.
Fever >72 h after effective antibiotic initiation.

managementGuide.title: MSSA practical guide
definition: Methicillin-susceptible S. aureus is best treated with an active anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam when one is clinically appropriate; HPUSM specifically notes vancomycin is inferior to cloxacillin for MSSA.

siteRows.preferred: Cloxacillin; current NAG quick guide also lists cefazolin as preferred IV therapy.
siteRows.alternative: Use syndrome-specific alternatives for allergy/other constraints; uncomplicated oral options in the NAG quick guide include cephalexin or cloxacillin.

dosing: Open the linked drug monograph and syndrome card because dose/duration differ between uncomplicated skin disease, bacteraemia, endocarditis, bone/joint and CNS infection.
pearls: Do not continue vancomycin solely for convenience when MSSA is confirmed and a suitable beta-lactam can be used.
Complicated S. aureus infection requires a search for deep focus/source and syndrome-specific duration.
managementGuide.duration: Use the actual MSSA syndrome duration; complicated bacteraemia/endocarditis/deep infection requires longer treatment than uncomplicated disease.
ipc: Use standard/local S. aureus infection-control measures according to clinical context.

resistance.name: NDM / Metallo-β-Lactamase Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Metallo-β-lactamase-producing CRE require a different strategy from KPC/OXA-48-like disease because avibactam does not inhibit the MBL itself.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam given simultaneously as a preferred regimen, or cefiderocol as another preferred option.
bullets: Tigecycline high dose or polymyxin B are less-preferred alternatives in the source.
Avoid high-dose tigecycline for bacteraemia in the cited pathway.

managementGuide.title: NDM / MBL CRE guide
definition: NDM/VIM/IMP are metallo-beta-lactamases. Avibactam does not inhibit the MBL itself; the ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam strategy uses avibactam to protect aztreonam from co-produced serine beta-lactamases.

siteRows.preferred: Ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam simultaneously, or cefiderocol
siteRows.alternative: High-dose tigecycline (not for bacteraemia) or polymyxin B; severe/high-burden cases may need susceptibility-directed companion therapy.

dosing: MSIDC adult appendix: ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g IV q8h over 3 h; aztreonam 2 g IV q6–8h over 3 h. Adjust for renal function according to the source tables.
pearls: Administer ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam simultaneously in the cited pathway; the source states they are Y-site compatible.
Avoid high-dose tigecycline for bacteraemia because serum exposure is low.
managementGuide.duration: Use syndrome-specific duration and reassess combination therapy with clinical/microbiology response.
ipc: Use CP-CRE infection-control precautions and local screening policy.

resistance.name: Non-Carbapenemase-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: CRE can result from non-carbapenemase β-lactamase activity plus permeability changes. Some isolates remain susceptible to meropenem/imipenem despite ertapenem resistance.

sourceCards.title: Meropenem/imipenem susceptible non-CP CRE
sourceCards.text: If meropenem and imipenem MICs remain ≤1 µg/mL with ertapenem non-susceptibility, MSIDC recommends high-dose meropenem or imipenem using 3–4 h extended infusion.

managementGuide.title: Non-carbapenemase CRE guide
definition: Non-CP CRE has carbapenem resistance through mechanisms such as porin/permeability change combined with other beta-lactamases rather than a carbapenemase.

siteRows.preferred: High-dose meropenem or imipenem with 3–4 h extended infusion.
siteRows.alternative: If meropenem/imipenem are no longer susceptible, use the full CRE mechanism/site pathway.

dosing: MSIDC adult appendix: meropenem 1 g IV q8h for non-CNS infection; imipenem 500 mg IV q6h for usual non-cystitis infection, with prolonged infusion options in the source.
pearls: Do not call intrinsic imipenem non-susceptibility in Proteus/Morganella/Providencia CRE if the other carbapenems do not meet the definition.
managementGuide.duration: Use syndrome-specific duration; resistance mechanism alone does not lengthen the course.
ipc: Use local CRE infection-control policy and distinguish colonisation from clinical infection.

resistance.name: OXA-48-like CRE
resistance.summary: OXA-48-like carbapenemase phenotype. Use susceptibility testing and the CRE pathway rather than assuming all carbapenems or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors behave alike.

sourceCards.title: CRE mechanism-directed approach
sourceCards.text: MSIDC separates carbapenemase-producing CRE by mechanism and ceftazidime–avibactam susceptibility; use the CRE treatment algorithm and AST.

managementGuide.title: OXA-48-like CRE guide
definition: OXA-48-like enzymes are serine carbapenemases; phenotype can be difficult to infer from routine beta-lactam results, so carbapenemase identification plus AST is important.

siteRows.preferred: Use the CRE algorithm according to ceftazidime-avibactam susceptibility and infection site.
siteRows.alternative: If ceftazidime-avibactam is not active, use the mechanism-unknown/alternative CRE pathway with specialist review rather than assuming another beta-lactam will work.

dosing: When active and appropriate, ceftazidime-avibactam is 2.5 g IV q8h over 3 h in the MSIDC adult normal-renal table; adjust for renal function.
pearls: Do not extrapolate NDM treatment to OXA-48-like disease or vice versa; mechanism matters.
managementGuide.duration: Use syndrome-specific duration and clinical response.
ipc: Manage as CP-CRE according to local infection-control policy.

resistance.name: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
resistance.summary: Intrinsically resistant to carbapenems. Distinguish colonisation from infection and use susceptibility/site/severity to select therapy.

sourceCards.title: HPUSM targeted Stenotrophomonas pathway
sourceCards.text: First line: TMP-SMX 15 mg/kg/day by trimethoprim component in 3–4 divided doses for 7 days. If TMP-SMX/Bactrim is contraindicated, HPUSM lists ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h for 7 days.
bullets: Distinguish true infection from colonisation before treating.
The HPUSM ceftazidime alternative is source-specific; compare with the dedicated MSIDC Stenotrophomonas pathway shown on the same AbxHub page.

sourceCards.title: First question: infection or colonisation?
sourceCards.text: If the isolate represents colonisation, do not treat.

sourceCards.title: Treatment when true infection is present
sourceCards.text: TMP-SMX IV/PO is preferred. Cefiderocol or ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam are less-preferred source-listed options.
bullets: For moderate–severe infection, the source prefers combination therapy when using TMP-SMX or cefiderocol until clinical improvement.
Levofloxacin or minocycline may serve as a susceptibility-directed companion.

sourceCards.title: Tetracycline caveat
sourceCards.text: Because minocycline/tetracycline derivatives have low urine and serum concentrations, avoid them for UTI and use only in combination for bacteraemia.

managementGuide.title: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia practical guide
definition: S. maltophilia is a non-fermenting Gram-negative organism with broad intrinsic resistance, including carbapenems. Many respiratory/clinical isolates represent colonisation, so establish true infection before treatment.

siteRows.preferred: TMP-SMX IV/PO
siteRows.alternative: Cefiderocol, or ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam. For moderate–severe infection, MSIDC prefers combination therapy when TMP-SMX or cefiderocol is used, at least until clinical improvement; levofloxacin or minocycline may be susceptibility-directed companions.

dosing: TMP-SMX adult appendix: all-other-infection dosing is expressed by trimethoprim component (8–12 mg/kg/day IV/PO in 2–3 divided doses in normal renal function); renal adjustment is required.
Minocycline: 200 mg IV/PO q12h in the MSIDC adult appendix for Stenotrophomonas/CRAB companion use.
Ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam combination follows the CRE dosing/administration framework when selected; administer simultaneously in the cited pathway.
pearls: Do not treat colonisation.
Polymyxins have no established breakpoint for S. maltophilia in the cited guideline.
Tetracycline derivatives have low urine and serum concentrations: do not use them for UTI and do not rely on minocycline monotherapy for bacteraemia.
IV minocycline is not recommended for children <8 years in the source; neonatal TMP-SMX needs caution because of hyperbilirubinaemia/kernicterus risk.
managementGuide.duration: Use the clinical syndrome and response to determine duration. In moderate–severe infection, reassess the need for combination therapy once improvement occurs.
ipc: Standard precautions in the source; reinforce hand hygiene, equipment disinfection and environmental cleaning.

msidcIpcLink.title: IPC guideline for MDRO in healthcare settings

resistance.name: Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus (VRE)
resistance.summary: VRE requires confirmation of clinically significant Enterococcus infection, species and site. Current NAG quick guide lists linezolid as the preferred VRE agent; do not infer clinical efficacy from agents that may test active in vitro but are not clinically effective for Enterococcus.

sourceCards.title: NAG organism quick guide — VRE
sourceCards.text: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus: linezolid is the preferred agent in the current NAG Gram-positive quick guide.
bullets: Confirm infection rather than colonisation and identify E. faecalis vs E. faecium where possible.
Cephalosporins, aminoglycosides apart from high-level-resistance testing, clindamycin and TMP-SMX should not be interpreted as clinically active for Enterococcus based on apparent in-vitro activity.

sourceCards.title: Immunocompromised/febrile-neutropenia context
sourceCards.text: NAG notes linezolid as an alternative when there is no response to vancomycin and in suspected/confirmed VRE, VISA or VRSA.

managementGuide.title: VRE practical management guide
definition: Confirm Enterococcus infection versus colonisation, species, site and vancomycin susceptibility.
VRE phenotype removes vancomycin as a reliable treatment option; definitive therapy still requires syndrome and isolate-level susceptibility context.

siteRows.preferred: Linezolid (current NAG organism quick guide).
siteRows.alternative: Escalate to infectious-disease/clinical-microbiology review when linezolid is unsuitable, infection is endovascular/deep-seated, or susceptibility/clinical response is uncertain.

dosing: Use the linezolid monograph and syndrome-specific dosing/renal-RRT context; the NAG organism quick guide identifies the agent but does not replace syndrome-specific duration/monitoring.
pearls: Do not report or select cephalosporins, clindamycin or TMP-SMX as clinically active for Enterococcus merely because of apparent in-vitro activity.
Nitrofurantoin can be considered only for susceptible urinary Enterococcus isolates in the appropriate lower-UTI context; it is not systemic VRE therapy.
managementGuide.duration: Define by infection site, source control and clinical response; the organism quick guide does not provide a universal VRE duration.
ipc: Apply local VRE/contact-precaution and infection-control policy.

resistance.name: Community-Acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA)
resistance.summary: Community-associated MRSA is a clinically useful epidemiologic/phenotypic distinction for selected skin/soft-tissue presentations, but site, severity and susceptibility remain decisive. The current NAG Gram-positive quick guide lists oral/IV options for CA-MRSA.

sourceCards.title: NAG Gram-positive quick guide — CA-MRSA
sourceCards.text: Current NAG quick guide lists TMP–SMX or clindamycin as preferred CA-MRSA options; fusidic acid plus rifampicin is a listed oral combination, with linezolid or doxycycline as alternatives.
bullets: Do not use rifampicin as monotherapy.
Use susceptibility and infection-site/severity context; invasive disease should follow the appropriate MRSA syndrome pathway.

managementGuide.title: CA-MRSA practical management guide
definition: Community-associated MRSA is not a substitute for isolate susceptibility or infection-site assessment.
Use this layer mainly to expose current CA-MRSA quick-guide options and then move to the relevant SSTI/invasive-infection pathway.

siteRows.site: CA-MRSA skin/soft-tissue infection when systemic antimicrobial treatment is indicated
siteRows.preferred: TMP–SMX or clindamycin, guided by current NAG quick guide and susceptibility.
siteRows.alternative: Fusidic acid plus rifampicin is a listed oral combination; linezolid or doxycycline are listed alternatives. Do not use rifampicin alone.

dosing: Open the linked drug monograph and syndrome-specific pathway for dose, renal/RRT adjustment, interactions and monitoring; the organism quick guide is not a universal dosing table.
pearls: Drain/source-control purulent collections when indicated.
For bacteraemia, endocarditis, pneumonia, bone/joint or other invasive disease, use the relevant MRSA syndrome pathway rather than this SSTI-oriented quick layer.
managementGuide.duration: Define duration by infection site, source control and clinical response; the CA-MRSA quick guide does not provide one universal duration.
ipc: Apply current local infection-prevention policy for MRSA colonisation/infection.

checklist: Blood pressure stable with no unexplained hypotension
Functional gastrointestinal tract; oral fluids/food tolerated (NAG example: ≥1 L/day oral fluid or ≥40 mL/h enteral nutrition)
No vomiting, significant diarrhoea, malabsorptive disorder, short-bowel syndrome or swallowing disorder compromising oral absorption
An appropriate oral antimicrobial is available after considering bioavailability, interactions and allergy
No infection/source/device reason requiring continued IV therapy
Culture/susceptibility and total treatment duration/stop date reviewed
avoid: Bone and joint infection during the early phase
Undrained or inadequately drained deep abscess
Cystic-fibrosis/bronchiectasis exacerbation when prolonged IV therapy is required
High-risk neutropenia or severe infection during chemotherapy-related neutropenia
Melioidosis before at least 14 days of IV therapy
Septicaemia/critical infection with high mortality risk
Severe soft-tissue infection such as necrotising fasciitis or invasive Group A Streptococcus
Severely immunocompromised patient such as solid-organ or bone-marrow transplant when IV therapy remains required
notes: NAG states that liver abscess, adequately drained abscess/empyema, osteomyelitis and septic arthritis may be changed to oral therapy after ≥2 weeks IV in appropriate improving patients.
The conversion table gives usual adult doses for patients with normal renal function; renal/hepatic adjustment and syndrome-specific dosing still apply.

hypoalbuminaemia.name: Hypoalbuminaemia (albumin ≤25 g/L)
hypoalbuminaemia.summary: Highly protein-bound antimicrobials may have increased free fraction, volume of distribution and clearance, reducing exposure despite a higher unbound fraction.
principles: Avoid ertapenem in critically ill patients with marked hypoalbuminaemia in the cited MSIC appendix.
Use drug-specific loading/maintenance or TDM strategies rather than reducing dose solely because albumin is low.

obesity.name: Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
obesity.summary: Dosing weight depends on antimicrobial properties. Volume of distribution informs loading dose; clearance informs maintenance dose.
principles: MSIC defines AdjBW = IBW + 0.4 × (ABW − IBW).
IBW: male 50 + 0.91 × (height cm −152.4); female 45.5 + 0.91 × (height cm −152.4).
Drug-specific obesity recommendations should supersede generic weight rules.

ecmo.name: ECMO
ecmo.summary: ECMO can alter antimicrobial pharmacokinetics through circuit sequestration, haemodilution, altered volume of distribution and drug elimination; available antibiotic dosing data are limited.
principles: Use standard/critical-illness loading exposure unless a drug-specific source states otherwise.
Prioritise TDM when available for narrow-therapeutic-index agents.

augmented-renal-clearance.name: Augmented renal clearance (ARC)
augmented-renal-clearance.summary: Critical illness can produce renal clearance above normal, risking subtherapeutic exposure for renally eliminated antimicrobials.
principles: Use measured/estimated clearance and clinical context rather than assuming normal exposure at a “normal” creatinine.
MSIDC cefiderocol table includes a higher-frequency regimen for CrCl >120 mL/min.

cns-infection.name: Central nervous system infection
cns-infection.summary: CNS infection may require higher β-lactam exposure than non-CNS infection. The MSIC renal table explicitly provides high-dose meropenem and higher-dose cefepime/ceftazidime contexts.
principles: Do not apply a standard non-CNS dose to meningitis/ventriculitis without checking the syndrome-specific source.
Renal adjustment must preserve adequate CNS exposure while reducing toxicity risk.

sources.summary: NAG: AUC/MIC is the efficacy exposure metric; TDM is indicated when vancomycin is expected for >48 h, with more frequent monitoring when PK is unstable.
MSIC provides loading, renal/RRT regimens and sampling schedules; its ICU appendix lists AUC24/MIC target 400–600.

aucMethods: Bayesian software is described by NAG as the gold-standard estimation method.
An alternative NAG approach uses two concentrations (peak and trough) with analytic PK equations.
vancomycin.monitoringIndication: NAG: TDM for all patients expected to receive vancomycin for >48 h.
vancomycin.monitoringFrequency: NAG: at least biweekly in clinically stable patients; more frequent monitoring when pharmacokinetics are changing/unstable.
vancomycin.msicTarget: MSIC ICU appendix: AUC0-24/MIC target 400–600; infusion rate should not exceed 10 mg/min in its hypoalbuminaemia table.

msicSampling.normalRenal: Initial pre-level 30 min before the 4th dose and post-level 1 h after completion of the 4th dose in the cited MSIC approach.
msicSampling.crcl30to50: Initial assay 24 h after first maintenance dose.
msicSampling.crclBelow30: Initial assay 24 h after loading dose; subsequent dosing guided by TDM.
msicSampling.HD: If loading dose before HD, initial level 24 h after supplemental dose; if after HD, 24 h after loading dose.
msicSampling.CRRT: Pre-level 30 min before the second maintenance dose in the cited MSIC CRRT section; maintenance depends on MIC/effluent rate.

vancomycin.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED — NAG/MSIC principles preserved; AbxHub does not include an unvalidated single-level AUC calculator.
nagPaediatric: Neonates: 10–20 mg/kg/dose with interval q8–48h according to postmenstrual age, weight and serum creatinine.
Age 3 months–<12 years: 60–80 mg/kg/day divided; q6h is listed for normal renal function.
Age ≥12 years: 60–70 mg/kg/day divided q6–8h with normal renal function.
Paediatric CNS DRSP pathway lists vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses with target AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L.

maintenance: 500 mg q12h when susceptible isolate MIC ≤0.5 mg/L
500 mg q8h when MIC ≤1 mg/L and CRRT effluent rate <30 mL/kg/h
1 g q12h when MIC ≤1 mg/L and CRRT effluent rate >30 mL/kg/h
msicCrrtRegimens.sampling: MSIC cited CRRT approach: pre-level/trough 30 min before the second maintenance dose.
msicCrrtRegimens.warning: These are source-specific example regimens, not an automatic dose calculator. Confirm actual CRRT modality/effluent, residual renal function, MIC and TDM.

workflowValidation.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED / PATIENT-SPECIFIC AUC CALCULATION REQUIRES A VALIDATED METHOD
requiredInputs: complete dose history with administration times
serum concentration value(s) with exact sampling times
acceptedSourceMethods: Bayesian AUC estimation (described by NAG as the gold-standard method)
doNotDo: Do not estimate AUC from a single trough using an unvalidated shortcut.
Do not reuse a previous AUC after a major renal/RRT or haemodynamic change without reassessment.

sources.summary: NAG describes extended-interval/single-daily dosing and lists patient groups where it is not appropriate, including pregnancy, CrCl <30 mL/min, dialysis, endocarditis and haemodynamic instability.
MSIC provides timed level sampling for single-daily and conventional aminoglycoside dosing and recommends more frequent monitoring with changing renal function/nephrotoxins.

aminoglycoside.pkpd: Concentration-dependent killing; NAG describes a target peak concept >10× MIC for EID/SDD.

msicSampling.singleDaily: After the 2nd dose: post-dose levels at 2 h and 6 h in the cited MSIC approach.
msicSampling.conventional: Trough 30 min before next dose; peak 30 min after completion of a 30-min infusion.
msicSampling.repeat: At least weekly when stable; more frequently with changing renal function or concurrent nephrotoxins.

aminoglycoside.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED FOR MONITORING PRINCIPLES — population-specific dosing and TDM rules remain separate.
aminoglycoside.nagChildrenMonitoring: NAG: in children, consider both peak and trough when renal function changes acutely or treatment failure is suspected; subsequent monitoring should be considered at least weekly.
aminoglycoside.neonatalGuard: Neonatal NAG CGA/PNA-based gentamicin/amikacin schedules are population-specific and must not be substituted with the adult EID/SDD nomogram.

workflowValidation.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED / NO AUTOMATIC NOMOGRAM REDOSING ENGINE
requiredInputs: serum level value(s) and exact sampling time
routingRules: If a NAG EID/SDD exclusion is present, do not apply a routine extended-interval nomogram.
Neonatal CGA/PNA schedules are a separate population pathway.
Gram-positive synergy dosing has different targets/monitoring from Gram-negative treatment dosing.
futureOptionalIntegration: validated aminoglycoside nomogram or PK service integration

records.name: Acyclovir
records.quickDose: NAG suspected HSV encephalitis: 10 mg/kg IV q8h; treatment duration commonly 14–21 days.
records.blueBookDose:
ADULT: 5 mg/kg by IV infusion 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 10mg/kg every 8 hourly in varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for at least 10 days in encephalitis; possibly for 14 - 21 days). 

NEONATE & INFANT up to 3 months with disseminated herpes simplex: 20mg/kg every 8 hourly for 14 days (21 days in CNS involvement), varicella-zoster 10-20mg/kg every 8 hourly usually for 7 days. 

CHILD, 3 months - 12 years: Herpes simplex or Varicella Zoster: 250 mg/m2 8 hourly for 5 days, doubled to 500 mg/m2 8 hourly for varicella-zoster in the immunocompromised and in simplex encephalitis (usually given for 10 days in encephalitis) | Indication (i)
Treatment for Herpes Simplex: ADULT - 200mg 5 times daily; In severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg. CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Treatment for Varicella Zoster: ADULT - 800mg 5 times daily; CHILD - 6 years and over: 800 mg four times daily, 2 - < 6 years: 400 mg four times daily, Under 2 years: 200 mg four times daily.

Indication (ii)
ADULT - Immune-compromised patients: 200 mg four times daily. Severely immune-compromised patients: dose can be doubled to 400 mg.
CHILD - two years and above should be given adult dosages, infants and children below two years old should be given half the adult dose.

Dosing is according to Product Information Leaflet.

notes: MSIC describes extended infusion over approximately four hours as a practical strategy for selected beta-lactams in critically ill adults when TDM is unavailable.

Preparation concentration is not a substitute for the indication-specific or renal/RRT maintenance regimen.

highRiskRRT.policy: AbxHub applies an RRT regimen only when it is explicitly structured in the cited source. Modality, effluent rate, residual renal function, infection site/severity and TDM can materially change exposure; when the source does not provide a regimen, AbxHub does not extrapolate one.

highRiskRRT.status: SOURCE-RECONCILED — source-specific RRT/CRRT rules and guards retained
highRiskRRT.effluentRateRule: CRRT is not a single dose category. Where a source gives modality/effluent-specific dosing (for example vancomycin), AbxHub shows it explicitly. Where the source does not provide a validated CRRT regimen, AbxHub displays a guard rather than extrapolating.
principles: Preserve/source-check loading or stat doses in critical illness; maintenance adjustment is a separate step.
Record modality (HD/CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF), actual effluent prescription, residual renal function, rapidly changing renal function and TDM availability.
Use concentration-guided redosing for high-risk narrow-therapeutic-index agents when the source requires it.
Do not convert a renal-dose table into a prescription without indication/site/MIC context.

colistin.sourceRule: MSIC and MSIDC use MU-based dosing with renal/HD/CRRT schedules. Stop CRRT-specific regimen when CRRT stops.

principles: Use prophylaxis only when a procedure/patient risk warrants it.

Give the first dose so adequate tissue concentration is present at incision; most standard agents are administered within 60 minutes before incision, while longer infusions such as vancomycin should begin earlier.
Redose for prolonged procedures or major blood loss according to source-specific interval.
Avoid converting prophylaxis into unnecessary postoperative treatment; most prophylaxis is a single dose or ≤24 h unless the NAG procedure record explicitly states otherwise.

procedures.name: General cardiac surgery / valve / LVAD
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV; NAG cardiac-general record continues cefazolin q8h.
alternative: MRSA colonised: add vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV pre-op, then source-specified continuation.
Severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin.
comments: For bypass cases NAG notes an additional cefazolin dose may be considered at onset of bypass.

procedures.name: CABG / cardiac device insertion
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
comments: Cardiac-device insertion: single dose. CABG source record notes 24–48 h duration.

procedures.name: Thoracic surgery (adult A3 cardiac section)
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: MRSA colonised or severe beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV; clindamycin 600–900 mg IV is another allergy option.
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: General vascular reconstruction / AVF-AVG / aneurysm repair
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV with source-specified q8h continuation
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV
Severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin or vancomycin
comments: NAG distinguishes general vascular procedures from procedures where prophylaxis is not required.

procedures.name: Amputation of ischaemic limb
preferred: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Angioplasty / stent insertion
preferred: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis not recommended.
comments: Use treatment antibiotics only when a separate infection indication exists.

procedures.name: Gastroduodenal / oesophageal
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
Severe penicillin allergy: gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV; may add clindamycin 600–900 mg IV
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Appendectomy / small intestine
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
Appendectomy: amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV is an alternative.
comments: If appendicitis is perforated, switch from prophylaxis logic to treatment/source-control pathway.

procedures.name: Colorectal surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
When institutional MBP + oral prophylaxis is used: neomycin 1 g PO + erythromycin 1 g PO OR neomycin 1 g PO + metronidazole 1 g PO, three doses over the pre-op day window stated by NAG.
alternative: Cefoperazone 2 g IV OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
comments: Single IV prophylactic dose; oral component only with the source-specified mechanical bowel preparation strategy.

procedures.name: Hernia repair
preferred: Mesh repair: cefazolin 2 g IV.
No mesh: prophylaxis not routinely required.
alternative: Severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV
comments: Single dose for mesh repair.

procedures.name: Biliary tract surgery / hepatectomy
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV
Severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin or clindamycin + gentamicin
comments: Usually single dose; hepatectomy source record permits up to 24 h.

procedures.name: Splenectomy / left-sided pancreatic surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV
comments: Single dose; vaccination and longer-term post-splenectomy prophylaxis are separate issues.

procedures.name: ERCP
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
comments: Only when incomplete biliary drainage or obstructive biliary disease is present.

procedures.name: Clean craniotomy / spinal procedures
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
Vancomycin or clindamycin for source-specified allergy/MRSA contexts
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Clean with CSF shunt/implant
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Clean-contaminated / sinus-oropharyngeal breach
preferred: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV
Severe allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin + metronidazole
comments: Consider ceftriaxone 2 g IV if dura breach/CSF leak per NAG.

procedures.name: Operative vaginal delivery
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
alternative: Cefuroxime + metronidazole OR ampicillin/sulbactam OR amoxicillin/clavulanate
comments: Single dose after delivery.

procedures.name: Cesarean section
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV
Severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin 900 mg IV
comments: Single dose; selected major SSI-risk contexts may justify source-specified extension, max 2 days.

procedures.name: ERPOC / surgical termination
preferred: 1st trimester: doxycycline 400 mg PO single dose 1–2 h before procedure.
2nd trimester ERPOC: cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV.
alternative: 1st trimester: azithromycin 1 g PO 1–2 h pre-procedure.
2nd trimester: ampicillin + metronidazole or amoxicillin/clavulanate.
comments: Single-dose prophylaxis.

procedures.name: Hysterectomy / laparoscopy entering vagina or uterus
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
alternative: Cefuroxime + metronidazole OR ampicillin/sulbactam OR amoxicillin/clavulanate
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Intraocular surgery
preferred: Pre-op: povidone iodine 10% periorbital skin + 5% conjunctival sac.
Intra-op: intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg/0.1 mL.
alternative: Intracameral moxifloxacin 0.5 mg/0.1 mL (0.5%) is an off-label alternative in the NAG record.
comments: Use ophthalmology product-preparation safeguards; this is not systemic cefuroxime dosing.

procedures.name: Clean oral/dental surgery
preferred: Usually no prophylaxis; consider only when prolonged/high-risk/immunocompromised or where the procedure-specific NAG record indicates it.
comments: Do not prescribe antibiotics simply because a dental procedure is performed.

procedures.name: Major clean-contaminated / complex oral surgery
preferred: Benzylpenicillin 2 MU IV is one NAG option.
alternative: PO: amoxicillin 2 g OR amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.25 g OR cephalexin 2 g + metronidazole 400 mg.
IV: ampicillin 2 g OR amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g OR cefazolin 2 g + metronidazole 500 mg.
comments: Single dose; severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin 600–900 mg PO/IV.

procedures.name: Clean hand/knee/foot operation without foreign material
preferred: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis not recommended.

procedures.name: Closed fracture fixation / total joint replacement / spine / arthroscopy
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV
Severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin 600–900 mg IV
comments: Single dose.

procedures.name: Clean head & neck surgery
preferred: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis not recommended.

procedures.name: Clean-contaminated head & neck surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV
alternative: Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV OR ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV
comments: Use the source page for procedure-specific exceptions.

procedures.name: Clean plastic procedures
preferred: No routine prophylaxis unless patient/procedure has infection or poor-wound-healing risk factors.
comments: Examples include prosthetic material or prior irradiation as risk contexts.

procedures.name: Clean-contaminated cartilage procedures
preferred: Cefazolin 2 g IV
comments: Procedure-specific allergy alternatives should follow NAG Appendix 3.

procedures.name: Transrectal ultrasound / prostate biopsy
preferred: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV OR amoxicillin/clavulanate 1.2 g IV + gentamicin 3 mg/kg IV
alternative: Fosfomycin trometamol 3 g PO 3 h before, then 3 g PO 24 h after procedure
comments: Tailor to current local resistance and procedural guidance.

procedures.name: Laparoscopic urological surgery
preferred: Use the open-surgery recommendation according to clean versus clean-contaminated procedure.

nonSurgical.name: High-risk dental procedure in high-risk IE patient
preferred: Amoxicillin 2 g PO single dose 30–60 min before procedure OR ampicillin 2 g IV single dose 30–60 min before.
alternative: Non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity: cephalexin 2 g PO or cefazolin 1 g IV.
Severe penicillin hypersensitivity: doxycycline 100 mg PO or azithromycin 500 mg PO single dose 30–60 min before.
comments: Apply only to the NAG-listed high-risk cardiac patients/procedures; good oral hygiene remains essential.

nonSurgical.name: Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever
preferred: Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 MU IM every 4 weeks; consider every 3 weeks for high-risk group.
OR penicillin V 250 mg PO q12h.
alternative: Penicillin allergy: erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg PO q12h.
comments: Duration depends on carditis/residual valve disease: 5–10 years, age thresholds, and sometimes lifelong prophylaxis per NAG.

principles: Administer standard prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision; begin vancomycin within 120 minutes when used.
Maintain adequate intra-operative concentrations; redose if surgery exceeds approximately two antimicrobial half-lives or there is excessive blood loss.
In most paediatric procedures a single dose is sufficient and prophylaxis should not exceed 24 h unless the source explicitly states otherwise.
Weight-based maxima and age/neonatal qualifiers must be checked before administration.

procedures.name: Cardiac surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV; max 2 g; redose q4h.
alternative: MRSA/MRSE colonisation: vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV.
Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV, max 900 mg; redose q6h.

procedures.name: Clean-contaminated abdominal surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g; redose q4h.
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/kg of ampicillin component IV; redose q2h.
Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV + gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg IV.
comments: Examples include gastroduodenal procedures, early appendicitis and stoma closure.

procedures.name: Biliary tract surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g OR ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/kg of ampicillin component IV.
alternative: Ceftriaxone 50–75 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) OR cefotaxime 50 mg/kg (max 1 g), plus metronidazole 15 mg/kg IV; neonate <1200 g: metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg.
comments: Allergy: clindamycin + gentamicin.

procedures.name: Elective craniotomy / CSF shunt
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g; redose q4h.
alternative: Cefuroxime 50 mg/kg IV, max 1.5 g.
MRSA/MRSE colonisation: vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV.
Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV, max 900 mg.

procedures.name: Clean hand/knee/foot without foreign material
preferred: Prophylaxis not recommended.

procedures.name: Spine/hip/internal fixation
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g; redose q4h.
alternative: Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV, max 900 mg; redose q6h.

procedures.name: Clean procedure
preferred: Prophylaxis not recommended.
comments: Includes tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy/tracheostomy and listed clean procedures.

procedures.name: Clean with prosthesis
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g; redose q4h.
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/kg ampicillin component IV OR cefuroxime 50 mg/kg IV.
comments: Excludes tympanostomy tubes.

procedures.name: Clean-contaminated head & neck
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV + metronidazole 15 mg/kg IV.
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam OR cefuroxime + metronidazole.
comments: Allergy: clindamycin per source.

procedures.name: Elective soft tissue
preferred: No prophylaxis unless complex/prolonged; if complex: cloxacillin 25 mg/kg IV, max 1 g.

procedures.name: Cleft lip/palate or excision/grafting
preferred: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 30 mg/kg IV, max 1.2 g.
alternative: Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV, max 900 mg.

procedures.name: Non-cardiac thoracic surgery
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV; source max/day and q4h redosing apply.
alternative: Ampicillin/sulbactam 50 mg/kg ampicillin component IV.
Allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg IV.
comments: Includes lobectomy, pneumonectomy, segmentectomy, lung biopsy and thoracotomy.

procedures.name: Lower-tract instrumentation with infection risk factors
preferred: Trimethoprim 2 mg/kg PO, max 100 mg.
alternative: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g; allergy: gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg IV.

procedures.name: Clean entry into urinary tract / hypospadias
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g.
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 30 mg/kg IV, max 1.2 g.
comments: Treat UTI before procedure when possible; do not continue prophylaxis merely until catheter removal.

procedures.name: PEG/PEJ/nephrostomy or Tenckhoff catheter
preferred: Cefazolin 30 mg/kg IV, max 2 g.
alternative: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 30 mg/kg IV, max 1.2 g.

procedures.name: MCUG
preferred: Trimethoprim 2 mg/kg PO, max 150 mg; if already on UTI prophylaxis, NAG advises a therapeutic single dose before procedure.

procedures.name: Burns
preferred: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis not recommended.

nonSurgical.name: Rheumatic fever — secondary prevention
preferred: Benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM (>27 kg) or 0.6 MU IM (≤27 kg) every 3–4 weeks.
alternative: Penicillin V 250 mg PO q12h; allergy: erythromycin ethylsuccinate 15–20 mg/kg/dose q12h.
comments: Duration depends on carditis/residual heart disease and age, as specified in NAG.

nonSurgical.name: Infective endocarditis prophylaxis for high-risk procedures
preferred: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg PO (max 2 g) OR ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g), 30–60 min before procedure.
alternative: Allergy: clindamycin 20 mg/kg IV/PO (max 900 mg); cefazolin 50 mg/kg IV may be used in selected non-anaphylactic allergy contexts.
comments: Use only for NAG-defined highest-risk cardiac conditions and relevant procedures.

nonSurgical.name: Post-splenectomy prophylaxis
preferred: Penicillin V 125 mg PO q12h (≤5 y) or 250 mg PO q12h (>5 y).
alternative: Amoxicillin 20 mg/kg/day; allergy: erythromycin ethylsuccinate.
comments: Minimum 1–3 years post-splenectomy; selected high-risk/asplenic children need lifelong prophylaxis.

nonSurgical.name: Malaria prophylaxis
preferred: Chloroquine-sensitive area: chloroquine 5 mg/kg base weekly, max adult 300 mg base.
Chloroquine-resistant area: mefloquine weekly by NAG weight bands; age >8 y can use doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg daily, max 100 mg/day.
alternative: Atovaquone/proguanil daily by NAG weight bands, starting 1–2 days before exposure and continuing 7 days after return.
comments: Assess destination resistance and child-specific contraindications.

nonSurgical.name: Hib exposure
preferred: Rifampicin ≤1 month: 10 mg/kg PO q24h ×4 days; >1 month: 20 mg/kg q24h ×4 days, max 600 mg/dose.
comments: Indications depend on household/nursery immunisation and exposure circumstances.

nonSurgical.name: Meningococcal exposure
preferred: Ciprofloxacin single dose by age band.
alternative: Ceftriaxone IM stat OR rifampicin q12h ×2 days by age.
comments: Give to high-risk close contacts; tailor to index isolate susceptibility.

nonSurgical.name: Pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis
preferred: Azithromycin age-specific 5-day regimen.
alternative: Clarithromycin, erythromycin or TMP-SMX depending on age/contraindication.
comments: PEP is recommended for household and other high-risk contacts per NAG.

nonSurgical.name: Varicella post-exposure prophylaxis
preferred: Vaccination within 3–5 days for susceptible eligible contacts; VZIG/IVIG and delayed acyclovir strategy for source-defined high-risk susceptible contacts.
comments: Risk group and timing are critical; follow current varicella immunoprophylaxis guidance.

primaryCare.title: Acute Bronchitis and Pneumonia
triage: Differentiate uncomplicated acute bronchitis/viral illness from pneumonia.
Escalate for hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, sepsis, inability to maintain hydration/oral therapy, significant comorbidity or other red flags.
decision: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and antibiotics are generally not indicated.
If pneumonia is suspected, use age/severity-appropriate CAP pathway and assess need for hospital referral.

primaryCare.title: Acute Otitis Media
triage: Confirm acute middle-ear disease rather than otitis externa/OME.
Assess age, bilateral disease, otorrhoea, systemic illness, immunocompromise and mastoid/neurologic complications.
decision: Use observation/symptomatic treatment when the current pathway permits.
When antibiotics are indicated, use the age/formulation/duration details in the dedicated paediatric AOM record and current NAG algorithm.

primaryCare.title: Acute Pharyngitis
triage: Look for airway compromise, deep-neck infection, peritonsillar abscess, diphtheria features or severe systemic illness.
For uncomplicated sore throat, apply the NAG/Modified Centor approach rather than treating all cases.
decision: Use the dedicated NAG pharyngitis pathway when the bacterial-risk threshold is met.

primaryCare.title: Acute Rhinosinusitis
triage: Consider bacterial sinusitis with persistent symptoms without improvement, severe onset or worsening/double-sickening pattern.
Urgent referral for orbital/neurologic complication features.
decision: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral and should not receive antibiotics.
Use adult/paediatric bacterial rhinosinusitis pathway when clinical criteria are met.

primaryCare.title: Acute Gastroenteritis
triage: Assess dehydration, shock, dysentery, suspected cholera, severe immunocompromise and other invasive-disease features.
Prioritise oral/IV rehydration according to severity.
decision: Most acute gastroenteritis does not need antibiotics.
Use organism/syndrome-specific therapy only for severe/invasive/high-risk presentations supported by NAG.

primaryCare.title: Skin and Soft Tissue Infection
triage: Differentiate non-purulent cellulitis/erysipelas from abscess/purulent disease and necrotising infection.
Drain collections when indicated; urgent surgical review for necrotising infection or systemic toxicity.
decision: Source control is primary for abscess where appropriate.
Choose antimicrobial based on purulence, severity, MRSA risk, host factors and allergy; avoid antibiotics for minor conditions where NAG does not indicate them.

primaryCare.title: Urinary Tract Infection in Non-Pregnancy
triage: Differentiate uncomplicated lower UTI from pyelonephritis, complicated UTI and urosepsis.
Assess male sex, obstruction/instrumentation, renal impairment, recent resistant organisms and systemic illness.
decision: Use lower-UTI treatment only when symptoms fit cystitis without upper/systemic features.
Escalate to pyelonephritis/complicated UTI/urosepsis pathways when indicated.

primaryCare.title: UTI in Pregnancy — Asymptomatic Bacteriuria
triage: Confirm asymptomatic bacteriuria by pregnancy-appropriate urine-culture criteria and exclude symptomatic UTI/pyelonephritis.
Review gestational age, allergy, renal function and organism susceptibility.
decision: Pregnancy is a specific indication to treat confirmed asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Select an agent compatible with pregnancy and current susceptibility; use the linked NAG pregnancy and UTI records.

primaryCare.title: UTI in Pregnancy — Symptomatic
triage: Pregnant patient with fever, flank pain, sepsis, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral treatment requires urgent assessment/escalation.
decision: Use pregnancy-compatible lower-UTI therapy for uncomplicated cystitis and obtain culture.
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy requires a higher-acuity pathway and should not be managed as routine outpatient cystitis.

allergy.title: Antibiotic Allergy Evaluation
allergy.summary: Structured NAG Appendix 3 gateway for penicillin-allergy history, PEN-FAST risk assessment and source-directed challenge/referral decisions.

penFast.label: Anaphylaxis/angioedema or severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR)
Treatment was required for the reaction (or treatment history unknown)

allergy.nagLowRisk: NAG Appendix 3 uses PEN-FAST <3 as the low-risk screen for consideration of a supervised test-dose challenge in appropriate patients.
allergy.challenge: For appropriate low-risk patients, follow the current NAG test-dose challenge protocol and observation requirements; do not challenge patients with severe cutaneous or other high-risk histories outside an appropriate specialist pathway.
allergy.guard: This tool supports history/risk stratification. It does not override a documented severe delayed reaction, anaphylaxis, organ injury or specialist allergy advice.

specimen.title: Specimen Collection & Transportation
specimen.summary: NAG Appendix 5 principles for obtaining clinically meaningful microbiology before antimicrobial exposure when safe and transporting it correctly.
principles: Collect before antimicrobial therapy whenever this can be done without unsafe delay.
Use at least two patient identifiers and clearly document specimen type/site and clinical context.
Prefer tissue, aspirate or sterile-site fluid over superficial swabs when feasible for deep infection.
Avoid contamination by commensal flora and use aseptic technique.
Use the local laboratory’s current container, volume, temperature and transport-time requirements; consult microbiology for unusual/high-risk specimens.
checklist: Correct patient and exact anatomical site
Appropriate specimen type and sufficient volume
Relevant clinical details, travel/exposure and prior antimicrobials supplied

antibiogram.title: National Antibiogram — Interpretation & Limitations
antibiogram.summary: A cumulative national antibiogram can support empirical context but cannot replace patient-, site- and isolate-specific microbiology.
limitations: National cumulative data may not distinguish community- from hospital-onset infection.
An isolate included in a cumulative antibiogram may represent infection, colonisation or contamination.
It is less reliable for patients with recurrent infection, recent healthcare exposure or recent antimicrobial therapy.
Cumulative percentages do not provide the individual isolate MIC.
They do not incorporate infection-site PK/PD, allergies, contraindications, interactions or other patient-specific factors.
interpretation: Use local/institutional data when available and more applicable.
Match organism, infection site, severity and likely source before using cumulative susceptibility percentages.
Review prior cultures/colonisation and recent antibiotic exposure.
De-escalate or redirect when patient-specific culture/MIC data become available.

nagParityAudit.scope: Adult A1–A17; Paediatric B1–B14; Primary Care C1–C9; NAG appendices/information; named treatment-driving anti-infectives and pathogens.
nagParityAudit.method: Subsection-level reconciliation: a title match is insufficient. Coverage requires NAG decision branches, named treatment-driving pathogens, exact regimen/dose/route/frequency where NAG supplies them, alternatives, duration, age/severity distinctions, prophylaxis/source-control/diagnostic notes, or an explicit referral gateway where NAG itself delegates to another guideline.
nagParityAudit.primaryCareLimitation: C1–C9 are embedded official PDF flowcharts on the live NAG site. AbxHub retains first-class gateways and direct official links; the embedded PDFs are not redistributed or represented as verbatim copies.
nagParityAudit.copyrightApproach: AbxHub uses original structured summaries of clinical facts/regimens with direct NAG provenance links rather than reproducing NAG prose verbatim.
referralOnlyExamples: adult malaria/filariasis where NAG directs to external national/WHO guidance
nagParityAudit.namedOrganismExpansion: Added first-class pages for additional organisms explicitly named in NAG condition text where a clinically useful organism-level entry improves search/discovery; umbrella groups are retained where they are more appropriate.
nagParityAudit.finalSubtopicAudit: Added residual NAG subsection entities found by heading-level spot audit: A9 clostridial myonecrosis/gas gangrene and B3 pertussis PEP, plus first-class pages for named pathogens used in A4/A10/B3/B4/B9.

definitions.MDR: Non-susceptible to at least one agent in at least three antimicrobial classes (HPUSM wording).
definitions.XDR: Non-susceptible to at least one agent in all but two or fewer antimicrobial classes (HPUSM wording).
definitions.CRE: Enterobacterales resistant to at least one carbapenem or producing a carbapenemase; for organisms intrinsically less susceptible to imipenem (e.g. Proteus/Morganella/Providencia), HPUSM requires resistance to another carbapenem for this definition.

carbapenemaseContext: HPUSM notes NDM as a common Malaysian carbapenemase and lists KPC, VIM, IMP and OXA-48-like enzymes; NDM/VIM/IMP are grouped as metallo-beta-lactamases.
threeStepAssessment: Determine whether the isolate represents infection vs colonisation vs contamination.
Assess comorbidity and whether meaningful recovery from treatment is expected.
Assess clinical severity: stable/mild–moderate vs unstable/severe/critically ill.
hpusmXdroFramework.stewardshipNote: HPUSM states antimicrobial treatment is not required for colonisation/contamination. Its page-20 decolonisation/contact-precaution wording is reproduced as source content only; apply the current HPUSM infection-prevention policy for organism-specific decolonisation rather than treating this paragraph as a universal decolonisation order.
goalsOfCareContext: HPUSM asks clinicians to consider whether a terminal/progressive underlying disease, poor recovery potential or lack of feasible source control makes antimicrobial treatment non-beneficial and recommends supportive care/family discussion where appropriate. Apply patient-centred goals-of-care processes and current institutional policy.

hpusmGuide.title: HPUSM ASP 2025 — Guide to Antimicrobial Therapy
hpusmGuide.principle: Local HPUSM institutional guidance is retained as a distinct source layer. Full page transcripts support search and source verification; NAG/MSIC/MSIDC/Wellington recommendations remain separately attributed when they differ.

sections.title: HPUSM ASP 2025 sepsis / septic-shock bundle
sections.definition: HPUSM describes sepsis as potentially life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection and septic shock as sepsis with tissue hypoperfusion.
components: Measure lactate; remeasure when initial lactate >2 mmol/L.
Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension OR lactate >4 mmol/L.
Use vasopressor if hypotension persists during/after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP >65 mmHg.
timing: HPUSM states fluid resuscitation and antibiotic therapy should be initiated/completed within 1 hour.
HPUSM states all five bundle components should be completed within 3 hours.
additionalSourceText: HPUSM states at least 60 mL/kg fluid by 6 hours as an adequacy marker and asks clinicians to assess other causes of shock if hypotension persists despite that fluid resuscitation.
Other shock causes listed: bleeding, Addisonian crisis, cardiogenic shock, anaphylaxis and iatrogenic causes (e.g. antihypertensive therapy).
sections.safetyNote: These fluid-volume/timing statements are reproduced as dated HPUSM ASP source content (adapted there from 2018 sepsis literature). AbxHub does not turn the 60 mL/kg/6 h statement into an automatic fluid prescription; use current sepsis/critical-care guidance, dynamic reassessment and patient-specific fluid tolerance.

                       CHAPTER 1
          INFECTION, SEPSIS AND SEPTIC SHOCK

    Infection is said to have occurred when there is an inflammation as a result of invading
    microorganism. This inflammatory response could be localised or systemic. Sepsis is a
    systemic or whole-body inflammatory response to an infection. Specifically, sepsis can
    be defined as a potentially life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated
    host response to infection.

    Fever can be a cardinal feature of sepsis. Other common manifestations of sepsis in-
    clude tachycardia, tachypnoea, and confusion. Organ or source specific manifestations
    should always be sought, for example cough for pneumonia, or dysuria for a UTI. In a
    very young, old, and people with a weakened immune system, there may be no symp-
    toms of a specific infection and the body temperature may be low or normal rather than
    high.

    In short, sepsis is a condition when there is an infection (eg, infected wound) with sys-
    temic manifestation of inflammations (fever, chills & rigors, severe lethargy, temperature
    of more than 38oC, tachycardia and/or leucocytosis).

    At the other end of the spectrum, septic shock occurs when there is sepsis AND tissue
    hypoperfusion (eg, cold clamy peripherals, crt > 2s, hypotension and/ or lactate increas-
    ing).

    Septic shock is a medical emergency and thus requires immediate and accurate inter-
    ventions. These interventions are grouped together in sepsis bundle to guide clinicians.
    The five components of sepsis bundle are:

     Measure lactate level. Remeasure if initial lactate is > 2mmol/L.
     Obtain blood cultures prior to the administration of the antibiotics.
     Administer broad-spectrum antibiotic(s).
     Begin administration of 30ml/kg crystalloid for hypotension OR lactate > 4mmol/L.
     Apply vasopressor if the patient remain hypotensive during OR after fluid resuscitations
     to maintain MAP > 65mmHG.




                                            Adapted from: Intensive Care Medicine (2018) 44:925-928

6   ASP 2025                                      GUIDE TO ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY




    Initiation of fluid resuscitation AND antibiotic therapy must be completed within 1-hour.
    ALL five components of the bundle MUST be completed within 3-hours.

    The patient must have received at least 60ml/kg of fluid at 6-hours to be considered as
    receiving enough fluid resuscitation. Hence, the patients who have received adequate
    fluid resuscitation and yet remained hypotensive need to be investigated and or treated
    concurrently for other POSSIBLE causes of shock. Other causes of shock are;

     Bleeding
     Addisonian crisis
     Cardiogenic shock
     Anaphylaxis
     Iatrogenic (e.g, antihypertensive)

    It is important to realize that sepsis is a complication of an infection, and septic shock is
    a medical emergency which requires urgent intervention to avoid preventable deaths.
    In most cases, sepsis related deaths are due to the delay in recognition of sepsis, de-
    lay in initiation of an appropriate antimicrobial or failure to timely restore and maintain
    perfusion during therapy.

                           CHAPTER 3
                 HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED INFECTIONS
     Hospital-acquired infection (HAI) is also known as healthcare-associated infections
     or nosocomial infections. They are infections that the patients acquired while or soon
     after receiving health care, which are not apparently present or might be incubating at
     the time of admission. These infections are usually acquired after hospitalization and
     manifest 48 hours after admission to the hospital. It is important to differentiate it from
     community acquired infection because the types of pathogens and the resistant pattern
     of those pathogens may significantly differ with those responsible for similar infections
     acquired in the community.

     The pathogens commonly responsible for most HAI are;

       GROUP                  MICROORGANISMS

     bacilli

     Hospital acquired infections (HAI) include;
     Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI, CRI or CRBSI),
     Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI),
     Surgical site infections (SSI),
     Hospital-acquired Pneumonia (HAP),
     Ventilator-associated Pneumonia (VAP),
     Clostridium difficile infections (CDI).

     Risk factors for HAI are;
     Prolonged hospital stay
     Immunosupressive therapy
     Severe disease with multiple comorbidities
     Ventilator use
     The presence of invasive devices

15       ASP 2025                                GUIDE TO ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY


                          CHAPTER 5
               Staphylococcus aureus INFECTIONS
     Staphylococcus aureus (Staph) is a bacterium commonly found on the skin and in the
     nose of about 30% of individuals. It is the most pathogenic of Staphylococcus species.
     S.aureus causes the following conditions;

      (1) Superficial skin lesions (boils, styes) and localized abscesses in other sites.
      (2) Deep-seated infections, such as osteomyelitis and endocarditis and more serious
          skin infections (furunculosis).
     (3) S.aureus is a major cause of hospital acquired (nosocomial) infection of surgical
          wounds - and, with S. epidermidis, causes infections associated with indwelling
          medical devices.
     (4) S.aureus causes food poisoning by releasing enterotoxins into food.
     (5) S.aureus causes toxic shock syndrome by release of superantigens into the blood
          stream.

     MSSA

     Sensitive strains of S.aureus (termed Methicillin-sensitive S.aureus - MSSA) are com-
     mon cause of community and hospital-acquired bloodstream and invasive infections.
     Complicated MSSA infection requires infectious disease specialist consultation:

     a. Endocarditis
     b. Involving prosthetic devices
     c. Infection involving 2 or more organs/systems (disseminated infection)
     d. Positive blood culture > 72 hours after initiating effective antibiotic
     e. Fever > 72 hours after initiating effective antibiotic

     MRSA

     Staphylococcus aureus may show resistance to commonly used beta-lactam antibiotics.
     Alteration of penicillin-binding protein PBP2a leads to resistance to all β-lactam anti-
     biotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, beta-lactam/beta lactamase inhibitor combination
     and carbapenems). This is known as Methicillin-resistant S.aureus (MRSA).

     The infection rate of MRSA at HPUSM was relatively low, at 10.0 per 1,000 hospital ad-
     missions and showed a decreasing trend in recent years. (al-Talib et al, 2010). Risk fac-
     tors for MRSA include indwelling catheter, ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization,
     multiple comorbidities and severe underlying disease.

     Vancomycin is indicated for empirical therapy if MRSA risk is high, or the condition is
     severe. Infectious disease consultation is recommended. If antibiotic susceptibility test-
     ing showed MRSA, vancomycin is the drug of choice for the treatment. Meticulous hand
     hygiene and strict contact precautions are essential to prevent their spread.

     NOTE: However, vancomycin is inferior in terms of efficacy against MSSA, when com-
     pared to anti-staphylococcal penicillins such as cloxacillin, hence should not be used
     for MSSA.

16    ASP 2025                                   GUIDE TO ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY


                        CHAPTER 6
              MULTIDRUG-RESISTANT (MDR) AND
             EXTENSIVELY DRUG-RESISTANT (XDR)
                GRAM-NEGATIVE INFECTIONS

     MDR organism is defined as an organism which is non-susceptible to at least one (1)
     antibiotic from at least three (3) different classes of antibiotic.

     XDR organism is defined as an organism which is non-susceptible to at least one (1)
     antibiotic in all but two (2) or fewer classes of antibiotic.

     MDR and XDR organisms are resistant to multiple classes of antibiotics resulting in lim-
     ited choice of antibiotics for the treatment of infection.

     Commonly isolated MDR/XDR Gram-negative organisms:

     • MDR/XDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa
     • MDR/XDR Acinetobacter baumanii
     • MDR/XDR Enterobacterales

     These organisms may cause hospital-acquired infections in high dependency/intensive
     care settings.

     Meticulous hand hygiene and strict contact precautions are essential to prevent their
     spread.

19       ASP 2025                                 GUIDE TO ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY


                   CHAPTER 8
       CARBAPENEM-RESISTANT GRAM-NEGATIVE
                  INFECTIONS
     CRE can be defined as members of the Enterobacterales order resistant to at least one
     carbapenem antibiotic (i.e., ertapenem, meropenem, imipenem, doripenem) or produc-
     ing a carbapenemase enzyme. Resistance to at least one carbapenem other than imi-
     penem is required for bacteria intrinsically less susceptible to imipenem (e.g., Proteus ,
     Morganella spp., Providencia spp.).

     This CRE organisms belong to a heterogenous group of pathogens encompassing mul-
     tiple mechanisms of resistance. They can be broadly divided into those that are not car-
     bapenemase-producing and those that are carbapenemase-producing. The CRE which
     are not carbapenemase-producing may be the result of amplification of non-carbapen-
     emase B-lactamase genes (e.g., ESBL genes) with concurrent outer membrane porin
     disruption. The Carbapenemase-producing isolates account for 35%-83% of CRE cases
     in the United States, with higher percentages observed when restricting the definition
     of CRE to require resistance to meropenem or imipenem.

     The most common carbapenemases in Malaysia are New Delhi metallo-β-lactamases
     (NDMs), whereas in the US, the most common carbapenemases are K. pneumoniae
     carbapenemases (KPCs), which are not limited to K. pneumoniae isolates. Other carbap-
     enemases include Verona integron-encoded metallo-β-lactamases (VIMs), imipenem-
     hydrolyzing metallo-β-lactamases (IMPs), and oxacillinases (e.g., OXA-48-like)218-220.
     NDM, VIM, and IMP carbapenemases are collectively referred to as metallo-β-lactama-
     ses (MBLs).

     CARBAPENEM RESISTANT GRAM-NEGATIVE BACTERIA

     Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
     Carbapenem resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB)
     Carbapenem resistant Enterobacterales (CRE):
            Klebsiella pneumoniae
            E.coli
            Enterobacter sp.
            Proteus mirabilis
     Carbapenem resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa

     Initial approach to patients with suspected infection with extensively drug resistant
     organisms (XDRO):

     The Three (3) Steps;
     1. Determination of the status of the organism(s) isolated: Infection vs. Colonization vs.
     Contamination.
     2. Assess the patient’s comorbidity: Is the patient going to significantly recover from
     the treatment of this XDRO infection?
     3. Evaluate clinical severity: Stable or mild-moderate vs. unstable or severe to critically
     ill conditions.

20    ASP 2025                                    GUIDE TO ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY



     STEP 1: Infection vs. Colonization vs. Contamination

     INFECTION = Clinical, biochemical, and/or radiological evidence of infection;
       Requires treatment.
       Requires decolonization.
       Requires contact precautions.

     COLONIZATION = True culture results but not causing the infection;
      Does not require treatment.
      Require decolonization.
      Requires contact precautions.

     CONTAMINATION = The pathogen cultured does not originate from the patient;
      Does not require treatment.
      Does not decolonization.
      Requires contact precautions.

     STEP 2: Assessment of severity or risk of rapid deterioration. Determine whether the
     patient is clinically stable or unstable.
     Important parameters to consider in the evaluation of the patients in addition to the
     standard history taking, examination, and investigations, include:

     • Presence of bacteremia
     • Septic shock
     • Respiratory failure
     • Inotropic support
     • Requires ICU admission
     • Increasing ventilator settings

     STEP 3: Assessment of the patient’s potential to recover from the treatment of this
     infection

     The impact of the underlying illness can be so severe that a recurrent infection is in-
     evitable, and the treatment of one infection will lead to another infection with a more
     resistant organism or phenotypes. Therefore, the treatment of the patients with XDRO
     infection is generally not appropriate in the following situations:
         The patient who are terminally ill from a progressive, advance disease.
         The patient is not expected to recover with a reasonable quality of life upon the
         treatment of the infection.
         There is a no plan to remove the source of infection (i.e., no source control), making
         definitive cure impossible.

     In these situations, patients should be offered symptomatic and supportive care to en-
     sure comfort and minimize symptoms. The discussion with the family members are also
     strongly recommended for getting the advance directive in the event of further deterio-
     ration.

pages.text:
ANTIMICROBIAL STEWARDSHIP IN ICU
The dilemma of current antimicrobial use in ICUs is the balance between providing adequate coverage against
likely pathogens whilst minimising selection of antibiotic resistant organisms. The key aims of antimicrobial
stewardship (AMS) are to ensure the right drug is given at the right time, at the right dose and for the right
duration, aiming to eradicate infection whilst minimising adverse effects and costs.

A structured AMS program consisting of an interdisciplinary team, educational interventions, system innovations,
process indicator evaluation and feedback to healthcare workers is essential for successful implementation.
Appropriateness of a prescribed antimicrobial therapy can be assessed during AMS rounds or normal everyday
rounds.

The selective pressure that results from inappropriate use of antimicrobials highly correlates with the
emergence of resistance. Appropriate AMS consists of rapid identification and treatment of infections based on
pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic properties, avoiding the use of needless broad-spectrum agents, shortening
the duration of administration and minimising the number of patients receiving unnecessary antimicrobials.
Alongside the appropriate use of antimicrobials, rapid source control is equally important.

Optimal dosing should be individualised to the patient’s clinical characteristics, causative organism, site of
infection and pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of the antimicrobial agent.

Antimicrobial stewardship in the critically ill includes:

1. Rapid identification of patients with infection
   • A clinical diagnosis of infection should be made before administration of any antimicrobial.
   • Obtaining specimens for appropriate cultures before antimicrobial administration is essential to identify
		 responsible pathogens and enable de-escalation therapy. However, the results are often unavailable for
		 the first 24 hours.
   • The decision to start antimicrobials in a possibly infected patient needs to be balanced between the
		 uncertainty of infection and risk of delaying treatment against the overuse of antibiotics.
   • Biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) are available for clinical use in acute
		 infections, however their diagnostic accuracy is suboptimal and lacks sensitivity and specificity.
   • Molecular diagnostic testing may be used for timely and rapid identification of causative microorganism.

2. Ensuring appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy (AMT)
   • Empirical AMT should be based on regularly updated local data on the incidence of causative organisms
		 and their susceptibility to antimicrobial agents, for both community and hospital-acquired infections.
   • Recent antimicrobial exposure should be taken into consideration when initiating empirical AMT.

3. Minimising time to initial antimicrobial dose
   • The timing of initial therapy should be guided by the urgency of the situation.

• In critically ill patients with septic shock, febrile neutropenia or bacterial meningitis, empirical AMT should
		 be initiated immediately after obtaining microbiological specimens or even before, if the procedure is
		delayed.
  • In patients with possible sepsis without shock, appropriate specimens or investigations should be
		 obtained prior to AMT.

4. Optimising antimicrobial dose and interval
   Pharmacokinetic changes in the critically ill can be described as follows:

   Strategies that may be considered for dose optimisation include:
   • extended or continuous infusion of ß-lactams
   • once-daily dosing of aminoglycosides
   • appropriate dosing of antimicrobials with narrow therapeutic range e.g. Vancomycin
   • dosing of certain antimicrobials in special populations e.g. obesity, pregnancy
   • dose adjustments for patients with renal or liver dysfunction
   • dose adjustments for patients with hypoalbuminaemia
   • dose adjustments for patients on renal replacement therapy

 Factors affecting dosing in the critically ill include:
 ∙ Increase in volume of distribution (Vd) of hydrophilic antibiotics
		Vd of hydrophilic antibiotics (e.g. aminoglycosides, ß-lactams, Vancomycin, polymyxins) is increased in

patients with sepsis and burns. The increase in Vd can lower the plasma concentration during initial
		 therapy. Hence, administration of a loading dose is necessary to achieve appropriate concentration at the
		 site of infection.

  ∙ Hypoalbuminaemia
		 Hypoalbuminaemia is associated with a lower degree of protein binding in highly protein-bound
		 antimicrobials (e.g. Ceftriaxone, Cloxacillin, Ertapenem, Vancomycin) leading to altered pharmacokinetics
		 (PK). The increase in the free fraction (unbound) of the drug results in higher Vd and drug clearance. This
		 may reduce antimicrobial exposure and compromise pharmacodynamic target (Refer to Appendix B for
    dosage adjustment).

  ∙ Augmented renal clearance
		 Augmented renal clearance (ARC) [CrCl ≥ 130ml/min/1.73m2] is common in patients with sepsis, burns,
		 polytrauma, traumatic brain injury and febrile neutropenia. Eight-hour urine sample for creatinine clearance
		 may be collected to confirm ARC. Significant correlations between subtherapeutic concentrations of
		 ß-lactams or Vancomycin and ARC were observed. Hence, the dose of antimicrobials may have to be
		 increased and levels to be monitored.

  ∙ Extracorporeal therapies
		 In patients with kidney failure, the time to achievement of steady-state is increased for antimicrobials
		 cleared by the kidneys. Those on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) frequently have an
		 increased Vd. Hence, a loading dose is also necessary.

CRRT is effective at elimination of hydrophilic antimicrobials especially those with low protein binding.
		 However, the amount of antimicrobials eliminated depends on the mode, dose of CRRT delivered, blood
		 flow rate, filter material and surface area. Similarly, antimicrobial pharmacokinetics in sustained low-
		 efficiency dialysis (SLED) should be based on blood and dialysate flow rates, duration and filter surface
		area.

		 Time-dependent antimicrobials are more affected in SLED than in intermittent HD potentially resulting in
		 prolonged periods of concentration below minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Hence, supplemental
		 doses during or after SLED or prolongation of infusion times may be necessary. Antibiotic dosing
		 guidelines for use across all renal replacement therapy (RRT) modalities are not possible because of
		 varied drug clearances across the different modalities and settings.

		 There is limited data on optimal dosing for antibiotics in the presence of extracorporeal membrane
		 oxygenation (ECMO). Common mechanisms that influence pharmacokinetics during ECMO are
		 sequestration in the circuit, increased Vd, decreased drug elimination and direct adsorption to the
		 membrane. Hydrophilic antibiotics with a small Vd are prone to haemodilution and direct adsorption by the
		 membrane. In contrast, lipophilic and highly protein-bound antimicrobials (e.g. Voriconazole) with a large
		Vd are sequestered in the circuit.

5. De-escalation of therapy
   • Antimicrobial de-escalation refers to a strategy of replacing a broad-spectrum with a narrower-spectrum
		 antimicrobial targeting the specific organism from the culture available or discontinuation of antimicrobials.

• When culture and sensitivity results become available, choose susceptible antimicrobial with the
		 narrowest spectrum, least toxicity and most cost effective.
  • Discontinue empirical antimicrobial therapy if susceptibility testing or subsequent clinical correlation does
		 not support the presence of infection.

6. Appropriate treatment duration
   • A 7-day duration is generally appropriate for most patients including septic shock with or without
		 bacteraemia and those infected with multi-resistant organisms.
   • However, duration of treatment also depends on the type and site of infection, ability to attain source
		 control, general response to therapy and immune status.
   • Procalcitonin-guided therapy has resulted in shorter duration of antimicrobials in units where antimicrobial
		 duration exceeds 10 days.

7. Intravenous (IV) to oral (PO) antimicrobial conversion
   • Evidences have demonstrated the efficacy, safety and economic impact of IV to PO antimicrobials
		 conversion. IV to PO antimicrobials conversion also benefits the patient by eliminating adverse events
		 associated with IV therapy, increasing patient comfort and mobility as well as enabling early hospital
		discharge.

   Conditions that may be considered for PO conversion following adequate parenteral therapy:
   • Osteomyelitis
   • Septic arthritis

• Infected implant or prosthesis
    • Necrotising soft tissue infection
    • Complicated orbital cellulitis (abscess or other complication)
    • Intra-abdominal infection without deep-seated collections

    Conditions not recommended for IV to PO conversion:
    • Endocarditis
    • Central nervous system infections (e.g. meningitis, brain abscess, etc.)
    • Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia
